value.text: Lucie County voters will decide in November on two ballot questions aimed at addressing the county's growing population and its impact on infrastructure and services. The first question asks voters to renew the half-cent sales tax, originally approved in 2018, which is set to expire in two years. County leaders are seeking to extend the tax for another decade. This is not a new tax but would keep the total sales tax rate at 7%, with the half-cent portion funding infrastructure projects such as road improvements, sidewalks, stormwater drainage, and major projects like widening St. "Now we're seeing that impact, you know, the delayed maintenance and the increased growth we've seen picked up, we're starting to have to play catch-up with those infrastructure projects and the needs are still there," said Erick Gill, communications director for St. The second question focuses on expanding the mosquito control district to include the Tradition and southwestern areas of the county, which have grown beyond the current service boundaries. Currently, mosquito control services cover about half of the county's 600 square miles. If voters approve the expansion, affected property owners would pay about $28 more annually in taxes to fund fogging, spraying, and mosquito surveillance. Both measures will appear on the November ballot, addressing different needs as St. Lucie County continues to grow. Voters are encouraged to review their sample ballots to determine which questions apply to them before voting on Nov. A man in his 30s was found dead in a lake at Lincoln Park in Fort Pierce Wednesday morning, and police are investigating how he ended up in the water. An officer was flagged down by a citizen just after 9 a.m. who reported seeing a body floating in the lake near the 400 block of North 13th Street, Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said. Officers say they arrived and found a man face down in the water. Rescue crews pulled him out, but he was pronounced dead. Police identified the man but are waiting to notify his next of kin. Santiago described him as a Black man believed to be between 30 and 32 years old. Investigators are working to determine how the man entered the water and what he was doing before his death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified There were no apparent signs of trauma to the man's body, Santiago said, but he noted the body appeared to have been in the water for some time. Police are canvassing the area, speaking with potential witnesses and looking for surveillance footage that could help investigators determine how the man ended up in the lake, per FPPD. Santiago said investigators are also looking into whether currents in the waterway could have played a role in where the body was found. It is too early to determine whether foul play or drugs were involved. Investigators are waiting for the medical examiner's findings, including autopsy and toxicology results, to help determine the cause of death. CBS12 News will provide updates as more information becomes available.

Before heading to the polls for Florida's 2026 general election, voters should confirm where they are assigned to vote.Polling places can change between election cycles, and election officials recommend checking your polling location well before Election Day.Voters in Palm Beach County, St. Lucie County, Martin County, Indian River County and Okeechobee County can visit their local supervisor of elections website to verify registration information, view their sample ballot and locate their assigned polling place.Most county election offices offer online voter lookup tools that allow voters to:Verify voter registration statusView a sample ballotFind their precinctLocate their Election Day polling siteConfirm district assignmentsOn Election Day, voters must generally cast a ballot at their assigned polling location.During early voting, voters may use any authorized early voting location within their county.Voters should bring a valid photo ID with a signature.Those who arrive without acceptable identification may be eligible to cast a provisional ballot.

Lucie residents are being asked in a straw poll whether they would support paying more for an additional weekly trash pickup, with the proposal adding at least $131 annually to the residential solid-waste assessment. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Right now, residents receive one garbage pickup per week. The proposed change would increase costs by about $11 per month, with service potentially starting in 2028 if the city moves forward. “This is something that is nonbinding, but it gives City Council an opportunity to get a sense of the will of the people and what they would prefer to see,” said Scott Samples, spokesperson for the city of Port St. The city emphasized that the poll is not a final decision. A "yes" vote would indicate support for the additional cost, while a "no" vote would signal opposition. However, the results will not automatically change the current trash pickup schedule. City Council controls the trash contract and service levels, meaning any changes would require council approval and an updated agreement with the current waste management provider, FCC Environmental Services. The city also noted that a second pickup would be an ongoing expense and could increase with inflation. “City Council would take this up. They would have to work with the vendor to understand what the logistics of that would be. And then, the City Council would then vote on whether or not to move forward with this,” Samples said. The poll aims to provide city leaders with insight into residents' preferences, but the final decision will rest with the City Council. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Live music, hands-on arts activities, wellness experiences and family-friendly entertainment will take over the Kravis Center campus when its annual Block Party returns Saturday, Oct. 17.The free event runs from noon to 8 p.m. at the Kravis Center for the Performing Arts and will feature performances, workshops and interactive experiences designed to connect the community through the arts.WATCH: Kravis Center Block Party returns to West Palm Beach"It's gonna be an amazing day, rain or shine, from 12 p.m. to 8 p.m.," said Lawrence Kaplan, one of the event's grand marshals. It's [going to] be extraordinary events, activities, kids' activities, and the music for all."Music will be a major part of the celebration, with performances scheduled across the campus.Among the performers is the Derek Mack Band, which will kick off the live entertainment."We're gonna be kicking off the festivities at 12:45, and it's gonna be live music all day long," said Derek Mack. "Me and my amazing band are going to put on a great show."The lineup also includes regional and local artists spanning a variety of musical styles, along with appearances by cultural organizations from across Palm Beach County.Organizers say the Block Party is designed to encourage participation, not just observation.Visitors will have opportunities to conduct musicians, explore instruments, participate in dance workshops, create crafts and enjoy family games throughout the day."We want to inspire the future Derek Macks," said Steven Sanders, another grand marshal for the event. "I think the way we do that is by getting kids to connect with the performing arts."Sanders said children will have an opportunity to experience activities they might not normally encounter."Get your child to experience conducting a symphony themselves, or decorate a magic wand and go and dance with real ballerinas," he said.The family-focused programming includes activities hosted by Ballet Palm Beach, Palm Beach Opera, Palm Beach Symphony and other community arts partners.One of the unique attractions returning this year is the instrument petting zoo, where visitors can get hands-on experience with musical instruments."The symphony's going to have its instrument petting zoo," said Bernie Pino, programming and rentals manager for the Kravis Center, while previewing the activities. "There's lots of things happening all day for kids of all ages, families, and adults too."Families can also enjoy crafts, games and interactive experiences hosted by community partners, including Rhythm & Hues."We have kids' games, arts and music on the second floor from 12 to 5, so come be happy with us, and we'll see you there," said Courtney Valle of Rhythm & Hues.A new addition to this year's Block Party is "The RESET," an immersive sound healing experience led by Chicago-based artist Davin Youngs.Participants are encouraged to bring yoga mats, blankets and pillows for the experience."Bring your yoga mats, blankets and pillows and enjoy a sound healing experience," said Oscar Quesada, the Kravis Center's senior director of programming.The wellness-focused event expands the Block Party's offerings beyond music and performance, giving attendees another way to engage with the arts.As families continue searching for affordable activities in South Florida, organizers hope the free event encourages more people to experience local arts organizations, discover new interests and connect with their community.The Kravis Center Block Party takes place Saturday, Oct. in downtown West Palm Beach. Admission and parking are free.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. If you've ever wondered what the world looks like through your dog's eyes or how your cat experiences its surroundings, a new exhibit at the Cox Science Center & Aquarium in West Palm Beach aims to provide answers.The new Cats & Dogs exhibition opened Oct. 10 and runs through April 16, 2027. According to the Cox Science Center & Aquarium, the interactive experience allows visitors to explore how cats and dogs see, hear, smell, communicate, and move through the world.The exhibition combines science, animal behavior, and hands-on activities designed to help guests better understand their four-legged companions. Visitors can compare their height to various dog breeds, test their balance by walking like a cat or dog, navigate agility challenges, and participate in games that highlight the unique abilities of household pets.One of the exhibit's central themes is encouraging visitors to "step into their pets' paws."Guests can explore sensory experiences that demonstrate how animals perceive the world differently than humans. Interactive stations examine body language, communication, physical abilities, and the ways cats and dogs use their senses to gather information about their surroundings.The exhibit also highlights the remarkable differences among breeds, allowing visitors to compare themselves to everything from Great Danes to smaller companion dogs and learn how physical traits affect behavior and movement.The exhibit was created to make science relatable through animals that many families already know and love.Visitors can participate in agility activities, balance challenges, and interactive games while learning more about animal intelligence, awareness, and communication. Organizers say the experience is designed for guests of all ages, whether they're lifelong pet owners or simply animal lovers.The exhibit arrives during a milestone year for the Cox Science Center & Aquarium.The center is celebrating its 65th anniversary and plans special community events throughout the fall. Upcoming activities include the center's Founders Day celebration, featuring educational experiences, community partners, and family-friendly programming.For South Florida families looking for educational attractions that combine learning with hands-on fun, Cats & Dogs offers a unique opportunity to better understand some of the animals that share our homes every day.The exhibition is included with general admission and is open through April 16, 2027.For additional information, hours and tickets, visit the Cox Science Center & Aquarium.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Dog lovers from across South Florida are heading to Fort Pierce this weekend for the Treasure Coast Kennel Club's Pirate Cluster, a four-day event featuring dock diving, FastCAT racing, agility, frisbee competitions, and other canine sports.The event is taking place Oct. Lucie County Fairgrounds, where visitors can watch trained canine athletes compete or give their own dogs an opportunity to try several activities. According to Treasure Coast Kennel Club President Lisa Root, many of the events offer same-day participation."It has to do with all kinds of sporting events that we do with our dogs, so dock diving, FastCAT, agility, UpDog (frisbee catching). It's fun," she said.Admission and parking are free for spectators. Fees apply for participants entering dogs into individual events.One of the most popular attractions is dock diving, where dogs run down a platform and launch themselves into a pool in pursuit of a toy.Competitors say many dogs recognize the venue before they even leave the vehicle."Once they start competing, they know what this dock means," said dock-diving participant Janet. "You'll see them when they start coming in. They just roll past the dock, and they'll start barking in the cars and stuff because they know that they get to get up here and just jump."Organizers say the excitement surrounding dock diving often becomes contagious for owners and spectators alike.In addition to the sporting events, the Pirate Cluster includes vendors, raffles and opportunities for families to spend time with fellow dog lovers.The event highlights the growing popularity of dog sports as a way for owners to stay active, build stronger relationships with their pets and connect with others in the community.Whether someone owns a highly trained competitor or simply wants to learn more about canine activities, organizers say the weekend provides an opportunity to see what these sports are all about.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Whether your idea of Halloween involves collecting candy with the kids or screaming your way through a haunted house, the South Florida Fairgrounds has an event designed for you.This October, the fairgrounds once again become home to two popular seasonal attractions: Spookyville, a family-friendly Halloween celebration at Yesteryear Village, and Fright Nights, a nighttime attraction featuring haunted houses, scare zones, rides, and entertainment.Spookyville transforms historic Yesteryear Village into a Halloween destination geared toward children and families.Guests can enjoy safe trick-or-treating throughout the village, costume parades, live entertainment, food vendors, and plenty of opportunities for festive family photos. The attraction's historic buildings are decorated with pumpkins, spider webs, fall decorations, and Halloween displays.Visitors can also enjoy rides, a petting zoo, balloon artists, and special performances. Among this year's entertainers is Wizard Aloysius, who brings magic tricks and family-friendly entertainment to the event on select dates.Spookyville runs Oct. 17-18, 23-25 and 30-31.When the sun goes down, the atmosphere changes dramatically.Fright Nights returns to the South Florida Fairgrounds with four haunted attractions, roaming scare actors, carnival rides, live entertainment, food vendors, and a midway designed to test visitors' courage.The event has become a Halloween tradition for thrill-seekers across South Florida and offers an alternative to traveling to larger attractions outside the area.During a behind-the-scenes visit, WPTV's T.A. Walker got a firsthand look at what it takes to become one of the monsters responsible for scaring guests. After receiving scare training, costume, and makeup, he attempted life as a Fright Nights scare actor under the pirate persona "Captain Arby's."The results were mixed.While a few guests played along, many walked by unfazed, proving that creating a memorable scare is much harder than it looks.Fright Nights runs October 15-17, 22-24, and 29-30.The South Florida Fairgrounds offers Halloween fans two distinctly different experiences throughout October. Families looking for safe seasonal fun can enjoy Spookyville during the day and evening, while older guests seeking thrills can test their nerves at Fright Nights after dark.Whether you're searching for treats or tricks, there's a Halloween adventure waiting at the South Florida Fairgrounds.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? The American Heritage Stallions are chasing a back-to-back 4A state football championship, and one of the players anchoring their offensive line has already secured his spot at the next level.Domenick Swanson, a senior at American Heritage in Delray, has committed to play college football at the United States Military Academy at West Point, New York.WATCH BELOW: American Heritage Delray offensive lineman commits to play football at Army"I will be going to West Point to play football," Swanson said. "It is a great opportunity. I went up there, and I was talking to coaches, and everyone says it's an amazing campus. I mean, it's such a great opportunity to join the military and serve my country and the ability to play college football. I'm very excited about it."Swanson wears No. 66 and plays center — a role he and his coach describe as the quarterback of the offensive line."You know, a big reason why our coach likes me at center is that it's like the leader of the offensive line. Being there for the guys and helping with all the plays, and it's a really important part," Swanson said.Swanson also has family support behind him, his cousin Lily, saying Swanson is a football superstar."Lily's my biggest cheerleader." Swanson said.As his high school career winds down, Swanson said what he will miss most is the bonds he has built with his teammates."Really just the relationships and bonds that I've made with my team. You know, I just, it's going to be sad to leave them all behind. Of course, you know, I'll always have my brothers, you know, we'll always be together, but playing football with them, it'll definitely be a big change." Swanson said.At the college level, Swanson said he looks forward to performing on a bigger stage and playing in front of thousands of people. Before he gets there, he has one goal left for this season."I would love to see us just go win every other game. That's kind of an obvious answer. But then, you know, we got our state championship. Hopefully we can go back-to-back," Swanson said.The Stallions are 7-1 heading into their Friday night game vs.

A shooting in the Banner Lake area of Hobe Sound on Wednesday night left one person dead, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. Deputies responded to the scene along Southeast Citrus Way and spent hours investigating. Authorities said one person was detained for questioning. Harriet Ford Greg, who said the victim was her grandson, shared that he lived with her. She recalled hearing three gunshots while she was in bed and immediately worrying about him, knowing he was out that night. When she stepped outside, she said she saw him on the ground as first responders tried to save him. " laying on the ground out there and the police officer was reviving him," Greg said. "I thought that he's not going to make it. Somebody shot him." Greg said she is trying to stay strong for her family but admitted she cannot bring herself to walk into the room where her grandson stayed, saying none of this feels real. The sheriff’s office is expected to release more information Thursday afternoon. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

The Palm Beach County School District's Advisory Boundary Committee (ABC) will hold a public meeting on Thursday, Oct. 22 to discuss proposed attendance zone changes affecting several elementary schools beginning in the 2027-2028 school year.WATCH: New $48 million school coming to Westlake, set to open August 2027The meeting begins at 6:30 p.m. at the Fulton-Holland Educational Services Center Board Room located at 3300 Forest Hill Boulevard in West Palm Beach.The proposed changes include establishing an attendance zone for a new elementary school — Elementary School "23-H" — in the city of Westlake, by adjusting portions of the Golden Grove Elementary and Loxahatchee Groves Elementary boundaries, the district said. Additionally, a portion of the Crystal Lakes Elementary attendance zone is proposed to be shifted to Sunset Palms Elementary.The district said the public may attend the meeting in person or offer input virtually. To register to give public comments virtually, visit the district's website and click the dropdown "2026-27 Advisory Boundary Committee (ABC) Meetings with Community Input." Meeting information, including the agenda and supporting documents, is also available on the district's website.The meeting will be livestreamed, recorded and posted here.

The Okeechobee County Sheriff's Office is asking for the public's assistance in gathering additional information regarding the movements of homicide suspect Earl Douglas Wadlington III prior to his arrest.WATCH: Sheriff, chief deputy announce arrest of wanted suspectWadlington was arrested early Thursday morning in Indian River County following an early-morning deputy chase. Deputies said a welfare check on 88-year-old Paul Eugene Baker, an Okeechobee County veteran, led to the discovery of his death and the arrest of Wadlington, the victim's grandson.Deputies are asking anyone who may have encountered Wadlington, observed him, or has information regarding his whereabouts between Sunday, Oct. 11, and his arrest in Indian River County on Thursday, Oct. 15 at approximately 3 a.m., to please come forward. Authorities said they are particularly interested in any sightings or interactions in Palm Beach, Martin and St. Lucie counties during this timeframe.WATCH: Suspect tracked down using license plate readers, deputies sayPhotographs show Wadlington on the day he left Okeechobee and at the time of his arrest, deputies said, and they want the community to pay special attention to the noticeable change in his hairstyle and overall appearance.Deputies said even the smallest detail could help investigators establish a more complete timeline of his movements.Anyone who saw Wadlington, spoke with him, or have any information that may assist in their investigation, please contact Senior Detective Ashley Rojas with the Okeechobee County Sheriff's Office at 863-763-3117 Ext 5108.

Having access to a gym is one thing. Actually using it is another.For Jennifer Fink, working out at home means avoiding some of the things she dislikes about going to a traditional gym.WATCH BELOW: Fitness at Your Door brings fitness trainers to your doorstep"I don't really like the gym, and I usually work out at home," Fink said. "You don't have to wait for machines or deal with people at the gym if you don't want to."It's one of the barriers Kashawn Fraser is trying to address through Fitness at Your Door, a South Florida wellness company that brings personal trainers directly to clients.Fraser said the company has grown to more than 250 certified personal trainers who undergo background checks, serving clients from Miami to Jupiter. The program is also expanding to the Treasure Coast."You can order Uber food to your door ... but to have someone show up for you where it matters the most, that's why this company was born," Fraser said.WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with Fraser to learn why he founded the organization.After playing professional football in the Canadian Football League and having multiple knee surgeries, he shifted his focus from his own fitness to helping others with theirs. "I had three reconstructive knee surgeries back to back," Fraser said. "I have been in your shoes. I've been hurt, I've been down, I've been out of shape, I've been in shape."For clients like Fink, having a trainer come to them can also take some of the anxiety out of going to a gym."You don't want to be on one of those YouTube videos where you are doing it wrong, and people are laughing at you," Fink said.The program also works with people living in 55-and-older communities. Fraser said staying active can be especially meaningful for people approaching retirement who want the energy to enjoy time with their families."You work so hard to get to retirement to enjoy your kids and grandkids and have the best energy you can," Fraser said.Across residential communities, gyms, fitness centers and clubhouses can go underused, even though residents have those amenities close to home. Fraser saw an opportunity to bring the workout into those spaces by having personal trainers meet clients where they already live.Click here to learn more about the program.

Palm Beach County voters now have a new way to check their voter information, find voting locations and track vote-by-mail ballots ahead of the 2026 General Election.Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections Wendy Sartory Link announced the launch of the free Vote Palm Beach mobile app ahead of Election Day on Tuesday, Nov. 3.>> SPECIAL SECTION: More election coverage, early voting locationsThe app is available through the Apple App Store and Google Play Store and is designed to give voters access to election information and services from their phones."Whether you're at home, at work, or on the go, we want to make it as easy as possible for every Palm Beach County voter to access accurate, reliable election information," Link said in a Friday news release.According to the Supervisor of Elections Office, voters can use the app to:Check their voter information and registrationFind voting locationsView election dates and deadlinesTrack a vote-by-mail ballotAccess information directly from the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections Office"With the 2026 General Election approaching, our new mobile app puts another trusted resource right in the palm of your hand," Link said. A welfare check on an 88-year-old Okeechobee County veteran led to the discovery of a homicide and the arrest of the victim's grandson following an early-morning police chase in Indian River County, Sheriff Eric Flowers and Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief said Thursday during a press conference.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff, chief deputy announce arrest of wanted suspectPaul Eugene Baker, a longtime Okeechobee County resident and veteran, was found dead on his property after his daughter-in-law called for a welfare check. His grandson, 35-year-old Earl Douglas Wadlington III, was taken into custody after deputies pursued him through a Walmart parking lot at approximately 4 a.m."What started off as a simple welfare check of an 88-year-old veteran in our county has turned into a tragedy and a family tragedy," Hazellief said.Baker's daughter-in-law had not seen or heard from him in several days. She went to his residence and found the house in disarray, which investigators said was highly unusual."She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazellief said.Law enforcement obtained and executed a search warrant for the property. Baker was found dead on the property. Investigators said the manner and location of his death made it immediately evident that it was a homicide.Baker's only vehicle was also missing from the residence, along with other property. Investigators learned that Wadlington had recently been living with Baker.The daughter-in-law told investigators that Wadlington had a history with the criminal justice system and that no other family member would allow him to live with them. Wadlington has over 800 felonies in his criminal background, the chief deputy said."The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazellief said.Because the daughter-in-law also held power of attorney for Baker, law enforcement was able to enter the missing vehicle into the ALPR system — a license plate reader network connected to partner agencies across the Treasure Coast area — as stolen. The vehicle was flagged as connected to a homicide suspect. Investigators tracked the vehicle leaving the area but chose not to issue a public alert."We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazellief said.WATCH BELOW: Dashcam video of chase, bodycam video of arrest in Indian River CountyInvestigators noted that while the agency was required this past month to remove Flock cameras from state roads and permitted locations per a state DOT order, cameras in other qualifying locations remained operational and allowed investigators to move forward with the case."To be specific with the language, we still have them in place in places that don't meet that criteria, and because of that, we were able to really move forward with this case," Hazellief said.Senior detective Ashley Rojas and her team led the investigation, the chief deputy said.The stolen vehicle was detected by Indian River County's Flock camera system this morning, leading investigators to the suspect's location.Indian River County Sheriff Flowers described the early-morning pursuit caught on video, in which Wadlington fled from deputies through a Walmart parking lot."One of the particular things that's interesting is it's 4 o'clock in the morning. He's running from our deputies. He's running through the Walmart parking lot. You see that our deputies were able to deploy stop sticks. The reason that he ultimately stopped and got out and ran is because his truck was going to stop working. That stolen vehicle is going to stop working," Flowers said.Sebastian Police Department also responded and assisted Indian River County deputies throughout the pursuit."Doesn't matter if the uniform is green or blue, doesn't matter what color it is. We're all going to go after the bad guys," Flowers said.Flowers praised the Flock camera system and said the county will continue using it despite public criticism."For all the naysayers and all the people who don't like flock and who don't like it, we're going to continue to use it. We're going to continue to put bad guys in jail because of it," Flowers said.Flowers noted that Indian River County cameras not covered by the state DOT order remain in operation. He said the Flock system has aided in other cases, including one involving a missing elderly woman.Wadlington was arrested on fleeing and eluding charges, deputies said, in addition to driving a stolen a vehicle. Both agencies said they are working very closely with the state attorney's office to obtain a warrant for his arrest for the homicide very soon."This guy is the definition of somebody who needs to stay behind bars," Flowers said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Residents along Brooklyn Lane in Lake Worth say their only road in and out of the neighborhood is deteriorating, raising concerns about whether emergency vehicles will be able to reach their homes."You know it's one way in, one way out, so we're in trouble," resident Gerald Hruby said.WATCH: Lake Worth neighbors fear deteriorating private road could cut off emergency accessFor neighbor Doug Rua, a former EMT and police officer, the biggest concern is public safety."I'm concerned about fire trucks being able to maneuver around it or over it, along with ambulances," Rua said. They said garbage pickup stopped when the road became too damaged for trucks to safely navigate.WPTV has been following the neighbors’ concerns. A West Palm Beach woman is facing a felony animal cruelty charge after investigators said her Yorkshire terrier was so severely malnourished that veterinarians gave the dog the lowest possible body condition score before it was euthanized.The investigation began Oct. 2 when Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control officers responded to Access Specialty Animal Hospital in Royal Palm Beach after staff reported a suspected animal cruelty case involving a 7-year-old Yorkshire terrier named King.Veterinary staff told investigators King arrived in critical condition suffering from severe emaciation, a heavy flea infestation and signs of prolonged neglect. According to the affidavit, veterinarians assigned King a 1 out of 9 body condition score on the Purina Body Condition Scale, the lowest possible rating, indicating extreme emaciation.The attending veterinarian told investigators the dog was non-responsive, severely hypothermic and in respiratory and cardiac distress when he arrived. According to the affidavit, the Yorkie was unable to breathe on his own. The veterinarian determined King's condition was the result of a chronic deterioration that developed over weeks or months rather than a sudden illness. Despite emergency lifesaving measures, including intubation and assisted ventilation, the dog's condition remained poor due to the severity of his condition. The veterinarian said the dog's emaciation as among the most severe she had encountered in her veterinary career and concluded King's suffering was most likely caused by prolonged neglect and a lack of adequate care.The affidavit states Marseille and another individual declined an advanced stabilization treatment recommended by the hospital because they could not afford the cost.Hospital staff identified Charlynn Marseille, 33, as the person who brought King to the veterinary hospital. Investigators later confirmed ownership through animal records and an interview at Marseille's West Palm Beach residence, where she acknowledged owning the dog.Investigators also referenced a 2023 complaint involving the same dog. According to the affidavit, a caller reported concerns that King had been left alone for days without food and was crying.Marseille was arrested Oct. 14 and charged with aggravated animal cruelty causing excessive pain or suffering. She is being held at the Palm Beach County

A man in his 30s was found dead in a lake at Lincoln Park in Fort Pierce Wednesday morning, and police are investigating how he ended up in the water. An officer was flagged down by a citizen just after 9 a.m. who reported seeing a body floating in the lake near the 400 block of North 13th Street, Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said. Officers say they arrived and found a man face down in the water. Rescue crews pulled him out, but he was pronounced dead. Police identified the man but are waiting to notify his next of kin. Santiago described him as a Black man believed to be between 30 and 32 years old. Investigators are working to determine how the man entered the water and what he was doing before his death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified There were no apparent signs of trauma to the man's body, Santiago said, but he noted the body appeared to have been in the water for some time. Police are canvassing the area, speaking with potential witnesses and looking for surveillance footage that could help investigators determine how the man ended up in the lake, per FPPD. Santiago said investigators are also looking into whether currents in the waterway could have played a role in where the body was found. It is too early to determine whether foul play or drugs were involved. Investigators are waiting for the medical examiner's findings, including autopsy and toxicology results, to help determine the cause of death. CBS12 News will provide updates as more information becomes available.

Lucie community members had a chance to learn more about and comment on proposed safety changes to Prima Vista Boulevard during a county information session at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center Thursday. The proposal focuses on the stretch between Aroso Boulevard and U.S. It would replace the center turn lane with a raised median and add landscaping designed to make the road feel narrower and encourage drivers to slow down. A majority of the community members spoke out against the plan, saying they don't believe the changes would improve safety. County officials say the changes are intended to improve safety, reduce crashes, and help slow traffic along the corridor. "We understand it's not popular. That's why we have these," said St. Lucie County engineer Dan Zrallack. "We're taking away the ease of access for people who live along this corridor. There's a lot of driveways. There's a lot of residences that have historically been able to turn directly into their driveway. It's no longer safe to do that. We have to control the traffic so that we have less accidents." County staff estimate the project could cost about $6.1 million dollars, but don't know where that money would come from yet. See also: Jupiter woman sues DoorDash, alleges delivery driver sexually assaulted her County leaders said feedback from the meeting will help shape the project. The proposal is in the early stages. Lucie County still needs to design the roadway, and identify funding sources before any work can move forward. Residents who couldn’t attend the workshop can review plans and submit comments to Christopher.arnold@stlucieco.gov.

A water tank at Jaycee Park has been transformed into a colorful tribute to Florida’s native wildlife thanks to Stuart-born and raised artist Christian Stanley and his wife, Jessica. "We keep an eye on the happenings that are going on here in Fort Pierce and saw that there was an open call to artists and put together a design that we thought was a strong submission and submitted it, and we're fortunately selected to come out here and paint the tank," said Stanley, co-owner of C. The decades-old, 22-foot-tall tank that can hold a million gallons of water is owned by Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. It was once a bright shade of white; now it features colorful paintings of manatees, dolphins, turtles, fish and pelicans, along with a sunset. "The great joy that I get out of being of mural artist is taking stuff from the ocean, from the forest, whatever, and bringing it out to the streets for people to see in a much larger-than-life fashion," he said. "So, when I knew the call was interested in being kind of native Florida wildlife, I knew that we could really bring something together that would be really impactful for the community." On Tuesday, Stanley and his wife traveled from Central Florida to the Treasure Coast to apply a UV clear coat to help protect the artwork against the harsh environment of the shore. The two originally began painting the tank in August, completing the mural within a month. He said they then decided to enter their work into Tnemec Company, Inc.'s 2026 Tank of the Year, not expecting much. But became the only South Florida water tank in the running against dozens across the state and the country. "We're so excited," Stanley said. "I think this is maybe our fourth tank, but yeah, definitely the first project that I've done that's kind of close to my hometown. And we're excited to be back and be a part of it. And it's really cool to be nominated. I hope that we have what it takes to be the winner, but we'll see." Stanley said it’s an honor to have their work recognized nationally, but he takes special pride in seeing it displayed in a place he still calls home: the Treasure Coast. "It's putting Fort Pierce Utilities Authority on the map in a really positive way," said Karyl Bertram, Environmental Laboratory Coordinator at Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. "We're very proud of our drinking water here. And yeah, it's just a really nice, warm feeling to know that we're being recognized for something as beautiful as this." According to Tnemec Company, Inc., one tank will be chosen by the public's vote, while 11 will be chosen by a committee of water tank enthusiasts. The people's choice voting closes on Friday, with the tank of the year expected to be announced next week.

Investigators in Martin County are working to determine whether a fatal shooting in the Banner Lake neighborhood of Hobe Sound was a crime or if the shooter acted within Florida's stand-your-ground law. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said the shooter told them he and his friend were on Southeast Citrus Way on Wednesday night when an argument escalated. According to the shooter, his friend repeatedly threatened to shoot him and even showed him a gun. "The deceased starts to pull out a handgun. The shooter pulls out his AR-15, actually, it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest, and he drops right there," Sheriff John Budensiek said. Family members identified the deceased as Jarvis Preston. The sheriff’s office has not released the identity of the shooter. "I know you're going to ask me, was it a stand-your-ground? And the answer is, I don't know right now," Budensiek said. Dave Aronberg, the former Palm Beach County state attorney who is not involved in this case but has experience with stand-your-ground cases, said the shooter’s account suggests it could fall under the law. "The shooter must have reasonably believed that firing the weapon was immediately necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm," Aronberg said. However, Aronberg noted that if Preston did not pull a gun, never had a gun, or if the shooter was the aggressor, the stand your ground defense would not apply. "You can't start a fight, provoke the confrontation and then shoot your way out of it," Aronberg said. The sheriff said investigators are still working to locate and interview witnesses to the shooting. He added that the final decision on whether charges will be filed will be made in collaboration with the state attorney’s office. "I know you're going to ask me, was it a stand your ground? And the answer is, I don't know right now," Sheriff John Budensiek said. Budensiek explained that Preston and the shooter were friends. Witnesses reported that Preston had been drinking heavily throughout the day and began threatening the shooter and others while armed with a gun. "He's talking, I'm going to shoot you, I'm going to hurt you. The shooter walks towards him, now they're at the edge of the road, at which point the deceased starts to pull out a handgun. The shooter pulls out his AR-15, actually it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest, and he drops right there," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the shooter called 911 and attempted life-saving efforts before Preston was flown to St. Mary’s Hospital, where he died. Preston’s grandmother, Harriet Ford Gregg, said she heard the gunshots and later saw her grandson lying on the ground. "It was Jarvis laying on the ground out there, and the police officer was reviving him," Gregg said. She shared her grief over losing Preston, who lived with her, saying his empty bedroom is now too painful to face. I'm not going in there," Gregg said. I visited Love, Hope & Healing Inc. to learn more about IGNITE: The Father & Son Grill Challenge, an event built around mentoring, communication and creating stronger relationships between young men and the adults who support them.While the event includes grilling and friendly competition, organizers say the larger goal is helping fathers, sons, mentors and mentees spend meaningful time together."We will have what we call the Fire Circle, where we will have a therapist-led session, and we're talking about some of these conversations that fathers and sons need to have, but rarely have and don't know how to have," said Donte Bates, co-founder and executive director of Love, Hope & Healing Inc. "So we're creating that space for them to actually talk about it."Yolanda Bates, CEO of Love, Hope & Healing Inc., said events like IGNITE help strengthen relationships that can have a lasting impact on young people."Fathers and sons, they need to create these bonds where these young men can have these experiences and the leadership and mentorship as they grow," she said.One of the organizations supporting the effort is United Way of Palm Beach County. Gwynette Williams, vice president of mentoring, said relationship-building is at the heart of the organization's mission."It's important to make sure that we are building relationships between adults and young people all over Palm Beach County," Williams said. "That's really what we do all day long."Williams also summed up one of the event's unique attractions with a smile."You can't go wrong with men and meat," she said.Mentor Bruce Lewis said his involvement is rooted in helping young men see a positive path forward."It's serving as a positive role model for the young African American males who really need that, giving them a good pathway to success," Lewis said. "I look forward to helping them build their futures."His mentee, Nate, said he's excited about both the experience and the opportunity to grow."I'm looking forward to making friends and having a better bond," he said.The event's presenting partner, Lowe's Home Improvement, is providing a grill and supplies for participating teams."We're in the community, and we're for the community," said David Territo, a Lowe's store manager.ABOUT IGNITE: THE FATHER & SON GRILL CHALLENGEOn Oct. 17, dozens of fathers, father figures, mentors, sons and mentees will gather at Gaines Park Recreation Center in West Palm Beach for IGNITE: The Father & Son Grill Challenge. Organized by Love, Hope & Healing Inc. and supported by Lowe's Home Improvement, the event uses grilling as a way to bring people together, creating opportunities for mentorship, teamwork and meaningful conversations. Along with a hands-on grill challenge, participants will take part in "The Fire Circle," a therapist-led discussion designed to help fathers and sons talk about topics that often go unspoken, from communication and accountability to emotional wellness and support systems. Three seniors at Alexander W. Dreyfoos School of the Arts have created Prodigy Pro, a free artificial intelligence platform designed to help students turn their ideas into real-world ventures.Co-founders Aiden Azoy and Anthony Tan and Head of Design Mia Rubio developed the platform after attending South Florida business networking events and realizing how few students were in the room.WATCH: Dreyfoos seniors build free AI platform for student entrepreneurs“We attended networking events and we noticed, why are we the youngest people in the room?” Azoy said. “There are so many talented students in our communities where they’re able to pursue their professional careers outside of school.”The students said they wanted to give young people a way to explore their interests, develop practical ideas and participate in West Palm Beach’s growing business community.The founders attend Dreyfoos in downtown West Palm Beach, where new development and the arrival of major companies have fueled the area’s growing reputation as “Wall Street South.”“We go to Dreyfoos, and literally hundreds of feet away are these huge constructions of Related Ross, companies like ServiceNow or even Citadel moving down to South Florida,” Tan said. “We’re right at the forefront of this new business center that is becoming West Palm Beach.”Tan said the students attempted to connect with professionals at local gatherings but struggled to find opportunities intended for people their age.“We tried to go to these meetings, and a lot of the time there wouldn’t be any opportunity for us,” Tan said. “So that’s why we wanted to create our own.”Prodigy Pro was built to help students take the first steps toward developing projects and businesses.“Prodigy Pro is a free AI entrepreneurship platform that helps a student take their idea from an idea to the final product,” Tan said.Azoy said the team created the platform after noticing that many students were not taking their ideas beyond the classroom.“Prodigy Pro is a way for students to build real ventures outside of school and be able to pursue their professional interests,” Azoy said. “We noticed that not enough students are getting out there and really putting their ideas out into the world. We gave them the ability to do that.”Users enter information about an idea and the problem they hope to solve. The platform’s AI then helps organize the concept and identify potential next steps.Rubio designed the user interface and worked to make the process understandable for students who may have little or no previous business experience.“You upload your information and the idea that you really want to pursue,” Rubio said. “And the AI will help you guide and shape and really tell you what your next step is, as well as create roadmaps, reminders and just really help your venture get off the ground.”The platform divides the development process into smaller sections and tasks.“With Prodigy [Pro], we wanted to make the next step super easy and attainable,” Rubio said. “So we grouped things into different sections and made each task super easy for the user to understand, so they know what to do next with their venture.”During a demonstration, the students used concerns about a school bus route to show how a user could enter a problem and explore possible efficiencies. “You input your information, and it really gives you the next steps, what you should do, and you can ask the AI to help develop your venture,” Rubio said.The founders said making Prodigy Pro free was central to their mission. Azoy said students should have access to the same entrepreneurial tools regardless of their school or community’s resources.“It’s completely free for students, and we want to stress that because we want to basically give the message that a student in an underprivileged school or community should have the same exact resources as, you know, a student in a resourced school,” Azoy said.According to the students, Prodigy Pro has grown to more than 15,000 users in 20 countries.The team also competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, a national student entrepreneurship competition.“A few months ago in May, we competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, where we won $7,500 for our venture,” Tan said.Tan said the prize money was reinvested into Prodigy Pro.“A lot of it went into the development of the platform, going through the UI, the back end, also enabling the AI to be free for other students,” he said.The three founders are seniors preparing for life after high school, but they said Prodigy Pro will continue.Asked whether the platform would remain after graduation, Rubio responded, “Yes, of course. It’ll remain to be a free platform for our users.”For Azoy, the larger goal is to show young people that they do not have to wait to begin developing their professional interests.“We really think that it’s important for them to be showing up and, you know, building ventures that really matter because every student has creativity in an underprivileged or privileged school,” Azoy said.The students’ work comes as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into education, business and everyday problem-solving. By making the platform free, the Dreyfoos seniors hope more young people will be able to turn their creativity into action and create opportunities of their own.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Jupiter Fire Rescue began its first day of municipal service Thursday by responding to four calls after midnight and unveiling Jupiter's first ladder truck, which carries a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10 and the six members who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.Fire Chief Darrel Donatto said the department's first calls unfolded as its members had prepared."They went perfectly, exactly as planned," Donatto said. "We've been planning for this moment for three years, and everything is perfect."The launch marks a new chapter for public safety in Jupiter, with locally controlled fire rescue and emergency medical services operating from stations serving the town's eastern, central and western communities.Jupiter's new ladder truck is based at Station 10, located at 500 N. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park. It is the first ladder truck based in Jupiter, according to Donatto.Donatto said the equipment is important because of the town's oceanfront high-rises and multi-story residential developments."Jupiter has a lot of high-rise buildings all along the oceanfront here, plus a lot of three-story type townhomes all through the Abacoa community," Donatto said. "And so a ladder truck is vital to protecting those, those type of occupancies."Palm Beach County Fire Rescue continues to serve nearby unincorporated areas, including county pockets near the Jupiter Inlet, DuBois Park and Jonathan's Landing, Donatto said.Jupiter's first ladder truck features an American flag design and imagery of the Jupiter Lighthouse. The truck carries the number 10 as a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10, whose firehouse sits across from the World Trade Center site in New York City.Following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, FDNY Ladder 10's replacement truck was wrapped in an American flag design honoring the firefighters who responded that day. Before adopting the tribute, Town of Jupiter officials contacted FDNY Ladder 10 to seek their blessing.Rodman Leas, a firefighter with Jupiter Fire Rescue, explained the significance behind the tribute."Today marks a brand new chapter in Jupiter fire history as we roll out 10 Truck, our community is, like you said, our community's very first ladder truck ever," Leas said. "It carries the number 10 badge ... as we honor FDNY Truck 10, whose firehouse stands directly across from the Sept. 11th World Trade Center site." Leas said six members of FDNY Ladder 10 made the ultimate sacrifice on Sept. 11."I took an inspiration from their American flag design as well ... as a constant reminder of the bravery, courage, brotherhood that defined the fire service," Leas said.Battalion Chief Jason Bohan said Jupiter Fire Rescue worked with Palm Beach Gardens as crews prepared for the new department's launch."We've had an incredible partnership with Palm Beach Gardens," Bohan said. "We've been using their training facility, and because of that partnership over the last couple of months, they and us have been training, getting ready for today."That preparation includes learning to put on approximately 60 pounds of protective equipment quickly when an emergency call comes in.Bohan said the most exciting part of launch day was bringing the new department together around its public service mission."Getting us all together, knowing what we're called to do, which is to protect and save people," Bohan said. "So now that it finally came today, we're all really excited."For Lt. Christian Lainhart, joining Jupiter Fire Rescue also represents a personal homecoming. Lainhart previously worked for Martin County Fire Rescue and described himself as a sixth-generation Jupiter pioneer."I'm super excited, very blessed to be here," Lainhart said.Lainhart said his family's roots in the Jupiter area extend to the 1890s. He grew up and attended school in Jupiter and is now raising his family there."It's just truly remarkable," Lainhart said. "Growing up here, I'm a sixth-generation pioneer, so that really means something here. Grew up here, went to school here, currently raising my family, and now I'm here serving the community that I know and love."While Jupiter's new stations, apparatus and equipment are central to the launch, Donatto said the department's personnel are what make the milestone meaningful."The most exciting thing is the people in it," Donatto said. "We've just been so incredibly blessed to hire some of the best people in the world. A program that has worked with thousands of Martin County children is returning after a brief hiatus, with a renewed focus on helping young students strengthen their reading skills. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County is celebrating the return of its AmeriCorps program, which places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support. WATCH BELOW: Literacy program returns to Martin County after hiatus “We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward,” Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County first introduced the federal mentorship program to the area in 2019. For six years, AmeriCorps volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause. Now, program leaders have set new goals for its return. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with AmeriCorps Program Director for Martin County Boys and Girls Club, Russell Lamberti. “We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar,” AmeriCorps Program Director Russell Lamberti said. AmeriCorps volunteers will work one-on-one and in small groups with kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys Girls Club locations, with an emphasis on literacy. For AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar, the mission also has a personal connection. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow,” Cesar said. The Boys Girls Clubs says the program delivered significant academic results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4. About the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization. The organization said students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns. AmeriCorps members’ work previously extended beyond the classroom. According to the Boys Girls Clubs, volunteers completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service. The return comes as literacy remains a focus across the county. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments. The AmeriCorps program is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs. The organization also provides after-school academic assistance through certified teachers. Beyond its Clubs, the organization runs or manages several programs serving local children, including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs. With AmeriCorps volunteers returning, the Boys Girls Clubs says it hopes to build on the program’s previous results while giving more Martin County students the individual attention and support they need.

WPTV is learning that potential road improvements are coming to a busy road in Port St. Lucie County staff are sharing designs and want to hear input from neighbors about a proposed project on Prima Vista Boulevard.WATCH BELOW: Neighbors weigh in on Prima Vista Boulevard changesThey plan to improve a section of the roadway from Airoso Boulevard to U.S. Highway 1 by removing the center left turn lanesDan Zrallack, county engineer, said their plan is to replace the center left-turn lanes with a raised median."The center turn lane is often referred to as a suicide lane," Zrallack said. A suspected fentanyl trafficker is behind bars after investigators say he sold drugs to a person who later died of an overdose, then led law enforcement on a high-speed chase that reached 115 mph and ended in Martin County. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro identified the suspect as 43-year-old James Arthur Green, who he said is a 10-time convicted felon. According to the sheriff, the investigation began after a fatal fentanyl overdose on Oct. Detectives used the victim’s phone to contact Green, who allegedly returned to the victim’s home Tuesday to deliver more fentanyl. Investigators say Green even sent a picture to the victim’s phone showing where he had left the drugs, unaware that he had been communicating with law enforcement the entire time. "Obviously, he didn’t know that this person had passed away. We were communicating with them," Del Toro said. Later that day, investigators say Green attempted to sell more fentanyl during an undercover operation. When detectives moved in to arrest him, Green fled, striking an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office cruiser before leading law enforcement on a pursuit down Interstate 95. Authorities say the chase reached speeds of 115 mph and continued into Martin County. The pursuit eventually ended near Kanner Highway after Florida Highway Patrol troopers deployed stop sticks and performed a PIT maneuver to stop Green’s vehicle. Del Toro emphasized the dangers of fentanyl and the importance of removing suspected traffickers from the community. This is killing our citizens and our community and preying upon people that have substance abuse problems," Del Toro said. "So I’m very, very happy this person’s off the streets right now." Green now faces multiple drug-related charges, along with additional charges connected to the pursuit. He is being held on a $440,000 bond. Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Wednesday. "The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," said Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn. Lenke sat motionless as he learned his fate. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," said Brandon White, Asst. "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served," said Justin Cormier, Asst. Lenke, 67, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter. A close friend of Richard Benson, who attended every day of the trial, had this to say about the sentence Lenke received. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," said Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop. Lenke did not testify in his own defense during the trial. Florida law requires the State Supreme Court to review every death sentence. So Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That process could take years.

A program that has worked with thousands of Martin County children is returning after a brief hiatus, with a renewed focus on helping young students strengthen their reading skills. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County is celebrating the return of its AmeriCorps program, which places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support. WATCH BELOW: Literacy program returns to Martin County after hiatus “We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward,” Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County first introduced the federal mentorship program to the area in 2019. For six years, AmeriCorps volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause. Now, program leaders have set new goals for its return. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with AmeriCorps Program Director for Martin County Boys and Girls Club, Russell Lamberti. “We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar,” AmeriCorps Program Director Russell Lamberti said. AmeriCorps volunteers will work one-on-one and in small groups with kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys Girls Club locations, with an emphasis on literacy. For AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar, the mission also has a personal connection. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow,” Cesar said. The Boys Girls Clubs says the program delivered significant academic results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4. About the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization. The organization said students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns. AmeriCorps members’ work previously extended beyond the classroom. According to the Boys Girls Clubs, volunteers completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service. The return comes as literacy remains a focus across the county. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments. The AmeriCorps program is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs. The organization also provides after-school academic assistance through certified teachers. Beyond its Clubs, the organization runs or manages several programs serving local children, including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs. With AmeriCorps volunteers returning, the Boys Girls Clubs says it hopes to build on the program’s previous results while giving more Martin County students the individual attention and support they need.

WPTV is learning that potential road improvements are coming to a busy road in Port St. Lucie County staff are sharing designs and want to hear input from neighbors about a proposed project on Prima Vista Boulevard.WATCH BELOW: Neighbors weigh in on Prima Vista Boulevard changesThey plan to improve a section of the roadway from Airoso Boulevard to U.S. Highway 1 by removing the center left turn lanesDan Zrallack, county engineer, said their plan is to replace the center left-turn lanes with a raised median."The center turn lane is often referred to as a suicide lane," Zrallack said. "The more turning movements you have, the more chances you have for accidents by restricting access and putting in the median turn lanes. We can kind of control where those turning movements are and protect the drivers as well as pedestrians walking along the roadway." According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, there have been 578 crashes on that section of the Prima Vista Boulevard since 2020. Zrallack said the median will make the road safer. "Statistically, the safety improves by up to like 40 percent or more," Zrallack said. But not every neighbor is sold on the improvements. Kadaysha Wilkins lives on Prima Vista Boulevard and told WPTV the median will make traveling more complicated. "Adding medians or anything else is going to cause more chaos than good," Wilkins said. "Ten to 12 years of living here, I've never seen an issue with our turning lane." Wilkins said it'll make it more difficult to take her niece and nephew to school by using the median instead of driving across the street. "A five-minute ride has turned into a 15-minute travel," Wilkins said.Wilkins said trying to come home could also be an issue."Turning into my driveway, which could have taken two seconds, is that now going to take 15 minutes?” Wilkins said. Zrallack said he hears the concerns and hopes they can address them on Thursday night during their public meeting."We're hoping to get more of that by hearing from the community again and seeing what else we can do to refine the design," Zrallack said.A second in-person public meeting for the project was held Thursday at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center.

In life, they say, take a leap of faith.Well, a group of kids in Stuart are doing just that on a diving board.WATCH BELOW: Stuart divers take leap toward big dreams"There are different things for different people. Some people prefer platform diving, which is much higher but fun, which I prefer. Something I’ve grown to love is all the friendships that I make throughout the years," said Grace Erickson, a local diver, who admits diving has always been her passion."On my preschool poster I wrote what I wanted to be when I got older was a diver," Erickson said.That preschooler who could only dream of being a diver is fulfilling her dream as an eighth grader."It’s been really exciting; it's new things every twist and turn, both in your head and diving off the board," Erickson said.Her longtime coach, Osvaldo "Pito" Alberty, thanks her for her courage and wants to see Erickson and her teammates take the sport to new levels."We are like a family here. We treat each other with respect and courtesy, and we push each other to do better than everyone else," said Pito, whose passion is sharing his experience, knowledge and love for diving with young athletes with the Atlantic Diving Team in Stuart.Atlantic takes divers of all ages, backgrounds and experience levels and teaches them the Olympic sport of diving."The younger we get them, the better it is because over time they can get scholarships. A water tank at Jaycee Park has been transformed into a colorful tribute to Florida’s native wildlife thanks to Stuart-born and raised artist Christian Stanley and his wife, Jessica. "We keep an eye on the happenings that are going on here in Fort Pierce and saw that there was an open call to artists and put together a design that we thought was a strong submission and submitted it, and we're fortunately selected to come out here and paint the tank," said Stanley, co-owner of C. The decades-old, 22-foot-tall tank that can hold a million gallons of water is owned by Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. It was once a bright shade of white; now it features colorful paintings of manatees, dolphins, turtles, fish and pelicans, along with a sunset. "The great joy that I get out of being of mural artist is taking stuff from the ocean, from the forest, whatever, and bringing it out to the streets for people to see in a much larger-than-life fashion," he said. "So, when I knew the call was interested in being kind of native Florida wildlife, I knew that we could really bring something together that would be really impactful for the community." On Tuesday, Stanley and his wife traveled from Central Florida to the Treasure Coast to apply a UV clear coat to help protect the artwork against the harsh environment of the shore. The two originally began painting the tank in August, completing the mural within a month. He said they then decided to enter their work into Tnemec Company, Inc.'s 2026 Tank of the Year, not expecting much. But became the only South Florida water tank in the running against dozens across the state and the country. "We're so excited," Stanley said. "I think this is maybe our fourth tank, but yeah, definitely the first project that I've done that's kind of close to my hometown. And we're excited to be back and be a part of it. And it's really cool to be nominated. I hope that we have what it takes to be the winner, but we'll see." Stanley said it’s an honor to have their work recognized nationally, but he takes special pride in seeing it displayed in a place he still calls home: the Treasure Coast. "It's putting Fort Pierce Utilities Authority on the map in a really positive way," said Karyl Bertram, Environmental Laboratory Coordinator at Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. "We're very proud of our drinking water here. And yeah, it's just a really nice, warm feeling to know that we're being recognized for something as beautiful as this." According to Tnemec Company, Inc., one tank will be chosen by the public's vote, while 11 will be chosen by a committee of water tank enthusiasts. The people's choice voting closes on Friday, with the tank of the year expected to be announced next week.

A nurse at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie is under investigation after allegedly stealing fentanyl from a critically ill patient’s IV bag on June 24 and 25, according to police. "They did an internal investigation where the Department of Health was then notified, in turn notifying PSLPD where we started our investigation in early August," said Officer Brittany McNally, public information officer for the Port St. Police said a family member of the patient reported seeing 54-year-old Leslie Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient’s fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket, and leave the room. "That’s not standard procedure, from what I understand at the hospital," McNally said. "But again, she’s not even assigned that patient. And there was no initial justification for her to even be in that room at the time." Investigators said Pope returned the following evening and approached the IV equipment again, but the family member intervened and stopped her. Hospital video reportedly showed Pope manipulating protective caps on the IV equipment, but investigators said she did not remove any fluid during the second incident. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 "The patient was on a specific monitor for the situation that he was in the ICU. And this individual had this monitor that had video recordings, which was a key piece of evidence in this case and completely contradicted what her recollection was," McNally said. Police said Pope denied the allegations and did not admit to using the fentanyl for personal consumption. "From my understanding, she did not admit that she was using it for personal consumption and essentially denied all the allegations that were made, but there was an overwhelming amount of evidence to prove otherwise," McNally said. Cleveland Clinic released a statement regarding the arrest, saying, "We take these allegations very seriously. The individual no longer works with us, and we are fully cooperating with law enforcement. Because this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this time." The investigation remains ongoing.
