WPTV is celebrating Hispanic Heritage Month, and we're sharing stories of the people and families helping shape our community.At the Guaranty Building in downtown West Palm Beach, history isn't just preserved inside the walls.WATCH BELOW: HISPANIC HERITAGE: Cuban immigrant family builds lasting legacyIt's part of the family story behind one of South Florida's architecture firms dedicated to preserving history.For nearly four decades, REG Architects has helped design, restore and preserve landmarks across the region whose work can be seen throughout Palm Beach County.But for co-founder Rick Gonzalez, the firm's story began with something much smaller."My father and I, in 1988, with zero money and two drafting tables, rented a very small office space, and we started," Gonzalez said.The company was founded by Rick Gonzalez and his late father, Ricardo Gonzalez, two Cuban immigrants who came to the United States with one suitcase.Together they built a business rooted in architecture, planning and historic preservation."One of the strongest influences was my father," Rick said. "I'd go to construction sites with him, and it was really cool to watch that."Rick remembers following his father to construction sites as a child, watching projects come together and developing a passion for the profession.What started as a small father-son business has grown into an award-winning architecture firm behind some of Palm Beach County's most recognizable projects. Over the years, REG Architects has worked on the restoration of the historic 1916 Palm Beach County Courthouse, which they helped uncover from the building that was constructed around it. They've also worked on projects at Mar-a-Lago, Trump International Golf Club, the Sandhill Crane Golf Clubhouse in Palm Beach Gardens and Havana Restaurant in West Palm Beach, where they got inspiration from a single postcard. Today, the firm is also working on renovations at St. Ann Catholic Church and School in West Palm Beach, expansion projects on the campus, and Spanish-influenced affordable housing developments for the West Palm Beach Housing Authority.Rick said his Cuban heritage continues to influence his work today."Oh my goodness, tremendously. I always loved Cuba and Havana in particular, the study of history and of the historic buildings in Havana," said Rick. "We use historical context when we design buildings. We want to make sure that we tie future building uses to the past."REG architecture prides itself on its diversity, giving credit for the success not just to the company's leadership but to the team working alongside them."We're very diverse, like America. So we have, we have an architect lady from Africa, we have several from Colombia, Cuban Americans, we have North Americans, we have people from everywhere, and that camaraderie, the working together, that's what makes an architectural firm great," said Rick.Today, that mission is being carried forward by the next generation.Rick's son, Ricardo Gonzalez, named after his grandfather, joined the company nearly five years ago and now helps lead the firm's business development and marketing efforts."It's such a legacy and an eagerness inside of me to preserve that," said Ricardo.Ricardo said the influence of his grandfather can still be seen in both the buildings his family designed and the values passed down through generations."He brought it from Cuba. He said, 'Here's our stamp, here's our footprint,' and it's there today," said Ricardo.For Ricardo, preserving history extends far beyond architecture."Continue on the legacies of your elders, your grandparents," said Ricardo. "Continue to tell those family stories."The family's story, which began with a small office, two drafting tables and a dream, now serves as a blueprint for future generations.Ricardo said Hispanic Heritage Month is an opportunity to celebrate culture while honoring the sacrifices and traditions that came before.For young Latinos looking to build their own future, Rick offers simple advice."I would tell young Latinos in general to follow your dream, and if you have an accent, don't worry about it," said Rick.He said success doesn't come from where someone started, but from the work they're willing to put in along the way."Your personality, the hardworking way that you are, is what's gonna get you ahead in this beautiful country," Rick said.For the Gonzalez family, preserving history means more than restoring buildings. It means ensuring the values, traditions and lessons passed down from one generation to the next continue to stand the test of time.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Department of Justice has threatened California with possible legal action over what it says are noncitizens believed to have received mail ballots for next month’s midterm elections.A letter sent Tuesday to Secretary of State Shirley Weber from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy U.S. attorney general, says the department has provided officials in Los Angeles County with a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election.California mails ballots to all registered voters.The letter obtained by The Associated Press gives the state 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are included on the list. For individuals whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received it. The letters warns that legal action may follow if the state does not meet the 48-hour deadline to review the list.“If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief,” the letter states.RELATED STORY | Records show ICE reviewed tens of millions of voter records looking for noncitizen votersA separate, similar letter was sent to the registrar's office in Los Angeles County, which the U.S. attorney's office had investigated during the state's June primary.Unclear how many names DOJ flaggedLos Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan confirmed in a statement that his office received the letter and a thumb drive, along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls.He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device and hasn't yet accessed any files. The letter, which Logan made public, does not specify the number of individuals flagged by the federal government.Logan said his office is working with the secretary of state and attorney general's offices to decide how to proceed. Neither of those two offices immediately responded to an emailed request for comment.“Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established,” Logan wrote. “And any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”Nationwide search for alleged noncitizen votersThe Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state.“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official,” Weber said in response.That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Young voter turnout could be pivotal in this year's midtermsAs part of its project to find noncitizens on the voter rolls, the Justice Department has been seeking detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. Some Republican-led states have turned over the information, which has been run through a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database that has been criticized as inaccurately flagging U.S. citizens.The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for that information, but so far has lost those cases in court. California is among the states that successfully sued, in part by arguing that turning over the data would violate state privacy laws.Election official calls 48-hour deadline “unreasonable”Santa Cruz County Clerk Tricia Webber, who is president of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, said she had not seen the letters but said the 48-hour deadline to vet voters flagged by the federal government was “completely unreasonable.”She said when there is a report of an ineligible voter incorrectly on the rolls, her office does due diligence to investigate. That involves looking at the voter’s registration history, identifying whether that person had voted before and, most importantly, reaching out to the voter, she said.“It would take more than 48 hours to even begin to get the full picture,” Webber said. She also questioned how the federal government came up with a list of alleged noncitizen voters since it doesn’t have access to the state's detailed voter information.Webber added that throughout the course of her decades-long career working for local election agencies, she has “never seen anything that would make me believe that our voter records are filled with fraudulent voters.”

Lucie family is turning unimaginable loss into hope after choosing organ donation following the death of their 14-year-old son , who was struck by a vehicle while walking to school, according to police. Lucie police said the teen was walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He died from his injuries two days later. Now, the family’s decision to donate his organs could help multiple people waiting for lifesaving transplants while creating a lasting legacy in his memory. Organ donation advocates say the family’s choice highlights an ongoing need for registered donors. According to transplant advocates, more than 100,000 people nationwide are currently waiting for an organ transplant, and 15 lives are lost each day while patients remain on waiting lists. The teen’s family chose organ donation in the days following his death, a decision supporters say can have a profound impact on recipients and their families. “It’s a courageous thing for them to do, and I think it’s the right thing,” said St. Lucie County Tax Collector Chris Craft. Craft has worked with Donate Life Florida through the tax collector’s office to encourage organ donor registration and raise awareness about the need for donors. For Tyre Gray, a kidney transplant recipient and the chief administrative and legal officer for South Florida Donor Network, the family’s decision carries special meaning. “Organ donation is one of the few places where grief and gratitude exist in the same place,” Gray told WPTV. Gray said he spent five years waiting for a kidney transplant before receiving the life-saving organ he needed. “I know for a fact that I wouldn’t be here without a family making that election in their deepest moment of despair,” he said. Gray described years of uncertainty while waiting for a match. “That’s five years of uncertainty, five years of being paralyzed, five years of not being able to grow,” he said. Organ donation advocates say the need for donors continues across Florida and the United States. Gray noted that a single donor has the potential to save multiple lives and help many more patients through tissue donation. “One donor is to save upwards of nine lives and to be able to heal another 75 lives,” Gray said. Behind those numbers are people awaiting a second chance, he said. “Let’s all be heroes and save lives,” Gray added. Advocates say organ donation often allows families to find meaning during some of life’s most difficult moments. “I would hope that they could see the lasting impact that a selfless act can make on others,” Craft said. “If you can help somebody else, it’s an amazing thing.” For transplant recipients, organ donation can mean more time with family, additional milestones and opportunities. In the midst of tragedy, one Port St. Lucie family’s decision could now help save lives and ensure their son’s legacy continues through the people he may help. Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Wednesday. "The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," said Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn. Lenke sat motionless as he learned his fate. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," said Brandon White, Asst. "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served," said Justin Cormier, Asst. Lenke, 67, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter. A close friend of Richard Benson, who attended every day of the trial, had this to say about the sentence Lenke received. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," said Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop. Lenke did not testify in his own defense during the trial. Florida law requires the State Supreme Court to review every death sentence. So Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That process could take years.

A 54-year-old Jupiter woman is facing felony charges after she allegedly removed fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV infusion while working at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said Monday. Pope was booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on Thursday morning on an out-of-county warrant. She was released on Saturday morning after posting an original bond of $150,000. Pope is not an inmate at the St. "We take these allegations very seriously," Cleveland Clinic spokeswoman Rebecca Astorga told WPBF in a statement. "She individual no longer works with us, and we are fully cooperating with law enforcement. Because this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this time." https://www.facebook.com/PortStLuciePolice/posts/pfbid02W5HqPQihHo4JSGqHsePU1wjBMmTubGN5HyptojT8wtSJU5Pft8YBVYsKgckEN7mDl Port St. Lucie police arrested Pope after an investigation into the allegations. A recent change to a flight out of Vero Beach is sparking a bigger conversation about travel options on the Treasure Coast. Travelers tell WFLX that limited flight schedules and a lack of convenient transportation alternatives can make getting in and out of the area difficult, sometimes forcing them to drive to larger airports or rearrange their plans. At the Vero Beach Regional Airport, travelers shared their frustrations with WFLX reporter Brooke Chau about the challenges of getting where they need to go. “In the Treasure Coast area, Vero Beach specifically, it is difficult to get around,” said Peter Masella. He pointed to the lack of a Brightline station in Vero Beach, saying people often have to travel to other cities to access additional transportation options. A recent schedule change to Breeze Airways’ route between the New York area and Vero Beach has added to those concerns. The flight, which previously departed from Westchester, New York in the evening, now leaves in the morning. A New York City physician told WFLX the change has affected his work schedule. “I’m a physician working in New York City, and because of the change of flight for Vero Beach, I have had to rearrange my patients’ schedules two days in a row,” he said. Another traveler from Westchester, New York said the change can mean a longer trip. “Then I have to take a taxi all the way down and around to Vero Beach. It’s very inconvenient,” she said. However, Breeze Airways has also been adding destinations from Vero Beach. Last month, the airline introduced nonstop service to Trenton, Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Atlantic City, expanding the airport’s commercial flight options. Vero Beach Airport Director Brandon Dambeck says airlines regularly evaluate the performance of their routes, which can lead to new destinations as well as schedule or route changes. “All of these airlines are monitoring the routes and their gauge of success,” Dambeck said. For travelers, more destinations are welcome, but they say flight times that fit their schedules are just as important.

About one in five of them identify as LGBTQ. So, on a lot of issues that they feel touch on, their identities, or their rights, or their rights for their peers, their friends, their communities, that can be something really, really powerful for young people in terms of their ideology or their political views.”RELATED STORY | Barack Obama to campaign with Ohio Democrats as he expands his outreach ahead of Election DayGeorgia, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio all have competitive Senate races on the ballot, and that AYP survey found 60% of young voters in those states plan to vote for the Democratic candidate.There are nearly 50 million people between 18 and 29 years old who are eligible to vote in November, and that age group often leans Democratic. Medina said young voters are usually swayed by the issues, and their political leanings stem from a desire for change. “Almost half of youth under age 30 are young people of color. About one in five of them identify as LGBTQ. So, on a lot of issues that they feel touch on, their identities, or their rights, or their rights for their peers, their friends, their communities, that can be something really, really powerful for young people in terms of their ideology or their political views,” he said.Multiple surveys in 2026 show cost of living and economic issues are a top concern among young voters. They want to improve their own lives. And so they look at our political system and go, okay, ‘What's in the way of me having power?’ of me being able to affect change?’” Medina said.One advantage for politicians and advocacy groups – young voters are more persuadable than other voting blocs and they're willing to consider new ideas.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office (PBSO) has identified the robbery suspect involved in a deadly deputy-involved shooting incident that shut down a major Boynton Beach roadway for several hours Tuesday.PBSO identified the suspect as Gregory Dobkins, 51, of West Palm Beach.WATCH WPTV REPORTER MICHAEL HOFFMAN'S REPORT BELOW:The incident unfolded Tuesday afternoon near Woolbright Road, where a large law enforcement presence prompted the closure of the roadway in both directions. Martin County commissioners are moving forward with a proposed one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers, giving the county more time to study their potential impact before allowing new projects to move forward. The Board of County Commissioners unanimously approved the proposal on its first reading Tuesday, Oct. A second public hearing is scheduled for Oct. 27 before the moratorium can receive final approval. The proposed ordinance would temporarily stop the county from accepting new applications for large-scale data centers in unincorporated areas of Martin County. It would not apply to municipalities. Under the proposal, large-scale data centers are defined as facilities with an anticipated peak electrical demand of 50 megawatts or more. County officials say the pause would give them time to study concerns surrounding data centers, including noise, water usage, electricity consumption, wastewater disposal and potential environmental impacts. During Tuesday's meeting, officials also revealed that the county received an application for a data center on Monday, just one day before the hearing. See also: Florida drug trafficking bust leads to 19 arrests, 6 more suspects sought Applications deemed complete before the moratorium takes effect would be allowed to move forward under existing regulations. Commissioner Sarah Heard questioned whether 365 days would be enough time for the county to complete the necessary research. She also asked whether the moratorium could apply to smaller facilities using 20 megawatts or more of electricity. County staff explained that the 50-megawatt threshold comes from state law defining large-scale data centers. Commissioner Edward Campi said the county needs to hear from experts on both sides of the issue before making long-term decisions. Campi referenced a recent visit to Virginia, where he toured an area with approximately 120 data centers and observed their appearance and noise levels. He said the proposed moratorium would provide an opportunity for supporters and opponents to share their perspectives. Blake Capps also supported the proposal, saying the county needs to carefully consider where data centers could be located, including areas within its urban services boundaries. Commissioner Heatherington was absent from Tuesday's meeting. The county first directed its attorney to draft the moratorium in August as concerns grew over the potential impact of large-scale data centers. The proposal will return to commissioners for a second public hearing on Tuesday, Oct. If approved, the moratorium would give Martin County up to a year to review its regulations before accepting new applications for large-scale data centers.

October marks National Disability Employment Awareness Month, an annual observance recognizing the contributions people with disabilities make to workplaces across the country.The observance dates back to 1945, when it began as a weeklong national recognition of the contributions of people with physical disabilities. WATCH BELOW: Jupiter Goodwill employee celebrates 19 years on the jobIn 1988, Congress expanded the commemoration to a month, and it evolved to recognize the importance of increasing employment opportunities for people with disabilities, including those with mental health conditions and other nonobvious disabilities. Department of Labor's Office of Disability Employment Policy, created in 2001, now leads the annual observance. At a Goodwill store in Jupiter, that message can be seen through an employee who has spent nearly two decades putting his own talents to work.WPTV reporter Christy Waite spoke with Jeffrey McFadden Jr., who has worked at the Jupiter Goodwill for 19 years, but for him, going to work is about much more than earning a paycheck."I like to smile at others, uplift people and make other people smile," McFadden said.Staying with the same employer for nearly two decades is something he and his family take pride in."My dad said that is a big achievement, to be in a job for so long, and it's a blessing to be a part of this atmosphere and get to meet really nice people," McFadden said.He said his path into the workforce included attending Goodwill's transition school, where he received job training."I went to the Goodwill transition school where we get job training, and it helped us get jobs," McFadden said.Abra Joseph, the director of donated goods, said Goodwill's programs are aimed at helping people who face barriers to employment find and maintain jobs."Sixty percent of our team members self-identify as having some type of barrier to employment," Joseph said.She said the goal is to "create an environment where our team members feel valued, respected, and supported."But McFadden's talents extend far beyond his job.At 6 feet, 5 inches tall, Jeffrey has also made his mark on the basketball court as a Special Olympics athlete. He played center, has won multiple gold medals and earned Athlete of the Year honors in 2013."I got my awards and gave a Hall of Fame speech. I still remember that day," Jeffrey said.Perhaps that's the message at the heart of National Disability Employment Awareness Month: with the right opportunity, what's possible can be limitless.

Palm Beach County has recorded five deputy-involved shootings since the start of 2026, all of which ended in fatalities, including a deputy-involved shooting Tuesday that left a 51-year-old man dead.The latest shooting remains under investigation by the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office and its Violent Crimes Division, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office.The number of deadly deputy-involved shootings this year comes as law enforcement agencies continue to face heightened scrutiny over use-of-force incidents and transparency in investigations following fatal encounters.WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach County records 5 deadly deputy-involved shootings in 2026The first deadly deputy-involved shooting of the year occurred Feb. Secret Service agents and a Palm Beach County sheriff's deputy fatally shot 21-year-old Austin Tucker Martin near Mar-a-Lago.According to Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw, Martin breached the inner security perimeter while armed."He put down the gas can, raised the gun at a shooting position," Bradshaw said following the incident. "At that point in time, the deputy and the two (Secret Service) agents fired their weapons and neutralized the threat. He is deceased at the scene."Just days later, on Feb. 25, a Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputy fatally shot 44-year-old Charles Curtis McCloud Jr. in Pahokee.According to the sheriff's office, McCloud was accused of killing two men and injuring a third before attempting to strike a deputy with a vehicle and allegedly trying to fire a weapon at law enforcement.Sheriff Bradshaw later praised the deputy's actions."His training kicked in," Bradshaw said. With an 18-5 record heading into the playoffs, The Kings Academy volleyball team in Palm Beach County is one of the favorites to win the Florida state championship — and could also claim a seventh straight district title.Coming into this volleyball season, few teams in the state were talked about more than The Kings Academy, and for good reason.WATCH BELOW: Kings Academy volleyball team eyes state title"This year has been a year of expectations to win some stuff because our team is so well-rounded," setter Jordan Molnar said.Winning "some stuff" might be an understatement. The girls opened the season as one of the top teams in Palm Beach County and one of the favorites to win the state crown. Instead of feeding into the hype, the team came together with shared expectations."It's called the core covenant, and anytime they get a little sidetracked, we go back and refocus on those things that they said they wanted to do," head coach Bethafor Avila said. They wanted to get over the hump of losing in regional play and win a state championship, and while they're primed to do just that, the girls are taking it one day at a time and focusing on district play, where they could win their seventh straight district title."A lot of the girls on the team have been for a while, so we've got to experience a lot of those district wins. It's just special that we get to do it for such an amazing school," middle hitter Ava Maldonado said.At 18-5, the school might be amazing, but so are the Kings Academy volleyball team, who fully expect to put the entire state on notice."It's a lot of energy around because we know that we can do something big this year and we’re all just working hard to get to that," Molnar said."It's been fun; we have a great group of girls put together, and I think it's really nice to come together and compete with them," Maldonado said.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office (PBSO) has identified the robbery suspect involved in a deadly deputy-involved shooting incident Wednesday that shut down a major Boynton Beach roadway for several hours.PBSO identified the suspect as Gregory Dobkins, 51, of West Palm Beach.The incident unfolded Wednesday afternoon near Woolbright Road, where a large law enforcement presence prompted the closure of the roadway in both directions. PBSO previously confirmed that the encounter involved deputies and resulted in a death.WATCH WPTV REPORTER MICHAEL HOFFMAN'S REPORT BELOW:PBSO Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said the investigation began after a pizza delivery driver was robbed around 10 p.m. The suspect allegedly ordered a pizza to a Lake Worth location and told the driver he only had a $100 bill. When the driver pulled out money to make change, the suspect allegedly grabbed him, and the two struggled over the cash.The delivery driver provided investigators with a description of the suspect's vehicle and a license plate number, Bradshaw said.Investigators entered that information into license plate readers and received an alert Tuesday that the vehicle was in the Lake Park area.PBSO tactical units located the vehicle and conducted surveillance to confirm the registered owner was driving, according to Bradshaw. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.A PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said. Something was wrapped around his right hand, and deputies in the helicopter believed he might have been holding a firearm.Bradshaw said the man attempted to take cover behind concrete light poles as deputies tried to stop him using two types of less-lethal weapons. Three less-lethal rounds struck him but had no effect, according to the sheriff.Bradshaw said the man repeatedly yelled at deputies, "You're gonna have to kill me."When the man reached a second pole, Bradshaw said he got into a kneeling position and raised his hands in what appeared to be a shooting position.A deputy then opened fire, striking the man. He died at the scene.Officials said the investigation remains active and ongoing.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office and PBSO's Violent Crimes Division are investigating the incident.

It’s a long way from Washington, has a small population and hasn't backed a Democrat for Senate in nearly 20 years.Yet President Donald Trump on Tuesday devoted a big chunk of his dwindling time ahead of crucial midterm elections to head to Alaska — attempting to bolster a Republican incumbent senator in another sign of GOP fears about retaining control of Congress after Election Day on Nov. 3.Trump headlined a rally for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Wasilla, about 45 miles north of Anchorage — famous for being the hometown of former Republican vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin and the headquarters of the Iditarod sled dog race across the state.Trump's stop is part of a western swing also taking him to rallies in Arizona and Montana on Wednesday.The president noted to the crowd that he had flown eight hours to rally for Sullivan, whom he called “one of the best and most respected senators in D.C.” Sullivan, seeking a third term, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman who is running to put “Alaska first” and emphasizing cost-of-living issues.During Tuesday's rally, Trump announced that Taiwan would purchase gas from a proposed mega-gas project that he has been highlighting amid Sullivan's campaign and that it would invest more than $4 billion. There was no immediate confirmation from Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as its own. The White House did not immediately provide further details.Trump also said the Federal Communications Commission would vote in the coming weeks on investing an additional $162 million in expanding high-speed internet access in Alaska. And he announced pardons for two men who had pleaded guilty in 2022 to Clean Air Act violations for tampering with federally mandated monitoring devices on certain vehicles.Trump and Vance have been trying to boost Sullivan repeatedlyDemocrats last won a Senate seat in Alaska in 2008, and the state hasn’t elected a governor from that party since 1998. The only time Alaska didn’t vote Republican for president was during Lyndon B. Johnson’s landslide 1964 reelection.Yet high gasoline prices from the Iran war and persistently elevated inflation have damaged Trump’s approval ratings enough to leave Democrats dreaming of Alaska upsets.Alaska pollster Ivan Moore said he's seen a decline in Trump's support statewide that mirrors the president's falling approval ratings nationally. That means the Senate race may be decided by Trump 2024 voters who are now unsure they still back him.“The visit is certainly appropriate. Whether the visit will be effective or not is another matter," said Moore, who said when he first heard that Trump would visit Alaska, he didn't believe it would actually happen.The Trump administration has prioritized expanding oil and gas drilling in the state. Vice President JD Vance last week campaigned in Fairbanks for Sullivan and Republican Rep. Nick Begich.Sullivan recently joined Trump in the Oval Office, where the president announced a $54 billion investment by South Korea's government into the proposed Alaska gas project. That's despite South Korea saying the deal, and its total value, haven't been finalized.Versions of a gas project have been proposed in Alaska for decades.Trump trekking four time zones west to get to Sullivan’s home turf — an unusually long trip so close to the midterms — is his strongest show of support for the incumbent.Trump last campaigned in Alaska to try to defeat a fellow RepublicanAlaska is home to around 740,000 people, making it slightly less populous than Denver. It ranks 48th out of 50 states in population, smaller than all but Vermont and Wyoming.Trump nonetheless headlined a 2022 rally in Anchorage opposing Republican Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski after she voted to convict him on a charge of incitement of insurrection during his second impeachment trial, following the attack on the U.S. Capitol by a mob of his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021.Trump endorsed Kelly Tshibaka, who challenged Murkowski that year, but that didn't stop incumbent Murkowski from winning reelection.In Wasilla, Max Christensen was waiting in line for the rally and said he hoped to hear more specifics from Trump about the natural gas project, and said he was “really curious just to see how he’s going to handle things like inflation and gas prices and things like that.”Christensen, 22, said he thinks Trump has been a great president “despite all his flaws and stuff," adding, “I think he really does genuinely care about the people of the United States of America.”This year, there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballotTrump has complained about Alaska’s unique elections system. The state has open primaries, in which the four top vote-getters — regardless of party affiliation — advance to the general election, which uses ranked choice voting.RELATED STORY | Republicans are flooding Senate races with ad money, but paying a premiumThat's led to a scenario where there also will be another Dan Sullivan on the November ballot: retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, whom Trump and other allies of Sen. Sullivan have called a sham candidate. Sullivan has denied this, but Trump continued to hammer the other Sullivan at his rally.“They found a guy named Dan Sullivan, they put him up to get things a little confused,” Trump said, as he repeatedly urged his supporters to vote for “the real Dan Sullivan.”Trump also touted Begich, who is facing a competitive challenge from Bill Hill, an independent.Alaska has a history of rewarding candidates with an independent streak — something Vance acknowledged during his trip to Fairbanks last week."In very deep red years, Alaska is competitive. In very deep blue years, Alaska is still competitive,” Vance said. “I think it’s just a reality of the politics of the state.”Independence has been hard to find in the Republican Party, where Trump for years has had total control. Some Republicans facing tough elections have begun tiptoeing away from the president on key issues such as Iran and tariffs, but not Sullivan, who has been vocal in supporting both.Trump also questioned why three Republicans were running against a Democrat for governor and endorsed Bernadette Wilson, who finished third in the August primary but was the top vote-getting Republican. This came at the same time state GOP leaders — including outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy — are urging voters to rank Republicans on the ballot.Many Republicans — despite reservations with ranked voting — have seen a ranking strategy in that race as crucial for Republicans trying to win the seat.Trump's trade war with Canada may also be a factorTrump has also triggered a trade war with Canada, which shares a 1,500-plus-mile border with Alaska and is among the state's most important trading partners.The U.S. banned nearly $1 billion worth of imports from its neighbor — including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles — after previously imposing 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian products. Canada has responded with reciprocal bans and its own import levies, and the back-and-forth could raise prices for Alaska consumers.RELATED STORY | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumorsMaking Canada an enemy of sorts is "discomforting" for many Alaskans, said pollster Moore.“We associate, I think, probably more closely with the Canadians — more than a lot of the Lower 48," he said.

Lucie family is seeking justice after their German shepherd, Titus, was struck and killed by a truck in a hit-and-run incident last Tuesday on Goodman Avenue. "I want justice served because you didn’t stop; you killed my dog after you hit him," Michelle Baker, Titus' owner, said. Michelle and Dillon Baker, parents of two young children, are struggling to explain the loss to their 11-year-old son and 2-year-old daughter. The incident occurred around noon when the family’s dogs hopped the fence and ran down the road. Despite efforts to track them using GPS collars, the Bakers were unable to locate the dogs in time. "He knew he hit something because he stopped, then he kept going," Dillon Baker said. Surveillance footage shows a silver truck hitting Titus, stopping briefly, and then continuing to drag the dog down the road before running him over. "My dog did not deserve to go out like that," Michelle Baker said. The driver did not return to the scene, and animal control is investigating the incident as a hit-and-run. The family believes the act constitutes animal cruelty. "That’s a crime, that’s a full-on crime, it’s murder," Michelle Baker said. Back at the Baker home, Gypsy, who witnessed the incident, has not been the same since Titus’ death. The family has a message for the driver. "Pay attention, pay attention and care about what’s on the road in front of you," Michelle Baker said. WPBF contacted animal control for further comment on the incident; as of Monday night, they have not responded. WPTV Morning Anchor Ashley Glass is following up at the Resource Depot in West Palm Beach, home to a Let's Hear It community meet-up, and learning that the non-profit, which focuses on recycling and repurposing everyday items, just received a major boost in community support. "This place is amazing," Craig Goldenfarb, Esq., Founder and CEO of GOLDLAW, said. WATCH Local non-profit all about recycling gets community boostThe Resource Depot is one of 65 local non-profit organizations benefiting from the law firm's GOLDEN 100 program, in which $100,000 in funding was donated. "To support my community is really special," Goldenfarb said. "Putting money back into the non-profit is something that strikes me close to the heart.”Staff at the Resource Depot take in 20,000 pounds of donated materials each month and repurpose them for sale. Glass asked the Resource Depot's Executive Director, Jennifer O'Brien, how the funding will be used. "AI training for our staff," she responded. "We have a small but mighty staff, and we’re looking for ways we might work more efficiently.”O'Brien also told Glass that when the community is invested, it gives her entire staff the energy to keep pushing forward with their non-profit work and saving an immeasurable amount of what could be trash from landfills.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier highlighted the recent conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms at a press conference Wednesday, calling it the first major outcome from the state's newly created public corruption unit and warning that more investigations are underway across Florida.Speaking at the Attorney General's Office in West Palm Beach, Uthmeier said public officials who abuse their positions for personal gain will face increased scrutiny from his office and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE)."Public officials are held to an even higher standard," Uthmeier said. "If you work in a city hall, serve on a commission, if you hold public office or work for a state agency, you have a duty to serve the public and not use your job to enrich yourself."Last week, a St. Lucie County jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct, a third-degree felony, but acquitted him on a bid-tampering charge. The case centered on a city-owned parcel near the historic Lincoln Theater in Fort Pierce. Prosecutors alleged that in 2024, Mimms used his position to benefit a nonprofit organization on whose board his niece served by helping secure the land deal and later concealing his involvement. During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Mimms failed to disclose his familial relationship and took steps to influence and cover up the transaction.Uthmeier said the case represented the type of conduct the state's public corruption unit was created to investigate."The facts make clear that shenanigans took place to ensure that that nonprofit ended up with the award, and ultimately the city manager covered it up," Uthmeier said.According to Uthmeier, the nonprofit later received hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from a Catholic charitable organization for planned development on the property, though he said the infrastructure project never materialized."We'll keep digging," Uthmeier said. "I think more facts will come to light as to where that money was going."Uthmeier said since the public corruption unit was launched, investigators have opened more than 25 active public corruption investigations or cases statewide."This is the first big announcement," he said. "You'll see many to come in the weeks ahead as we wrap up our evidence and begin to press charges against people that have abused their office, that have abused the public trust."FDLE Larry Keefe said the agency is making public corruption investigations a top priority."When the people of Florida lose their sense of trust in their institutions, it's death by a thousand cuts," Keefe said. Sentencing for Mimms is expected at a later date."This will be the first of many, sadly," Uthmeier said. "I hope we don't have to do too many, but we'll do as many as necessary to ensure the public knows that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers, and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take."

A major stretch of South Ocean Boulevard in Palm Beach is scheduled to close Friday morning until further notice, prompting traffic changes for residents and commuters in the area. According to the Town of Palm Beach's website, South Ocean Boulevard (State Road A1A) will close between South County Road and Southern Boulevard beginning at 5 a.m. The closure will remain in effect until further notice.Town officials said information about traffic checkpoints, modified bridge-opening schedules and temporary marine security zones is available on the town's Planned Traffic Impacts webpage.The closure announcement comes as federal aviation officials issued a Temporary Flight Restriction, or TFR, for VIP movement in the West Palm Beach area. The notice is scheduled to take effect Saturday, Oct. 17, and remain in place through Sunday, Oct. 18.Similar road and airspace restrictions have been implemented in the past during visits by President Donald Trump to his Mar-a-Lago residence.At this time, neither the Town of Palm Beach nor federal authorities have publicly confirmed whether Trump is expected to be in Palm Beach this weekend.Motorists are encouraged to plan ahead and expect delays in the area surrounding the closure.

Lucie family is turning unimaginable loss into hope after choosing organ donation following the death of their 14-year-old son, who was struck by a vehicle while walking to school, according to police.Port St. Lucie police said the teen was walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He died from his injuries two days later.WATCH: Port St. Lucie Teen's Legacy Lives On Through DonationNow, the family's decision to donate his organs could help multiple people waiting for lifesaving transplants while creating a lasting legacy in his memory.Organ donation advocates say the family's choice highlights an ongoing need for registered donors. According to transplant advocates, more than 100,000 people nationwide are currently waiting for an organ transplant, and 15 lives are lost each day while patients remain on waiting lists.The teen's family chose organ donation in the days following his death, a decision supporters say can have a profound impact on recipients and their families."It's a courageous thing for them to do, and I think it's the right thing," said St. Lucie County Tax Collector Chris Craft.Craft has worked with Donate Life Florida through the tax collector's office to encourage organ donor registration and raise awareness about the need for donors.For Tyre Gray, a kidney transplant recipient and the chief administrative and legal officer for South Florida Donor Network, the family's decision carries special meaning."Organ donation is one of the few places where grief and gratitude exist in the same place," Gray told WPTV.Gray said he spent five years waiting for a kidney transplant before receiving the life-saving organ he needed."I know for a fact that I wouldn't be here without a family making that election in their deepest moment of despair," he said.Gray described years of uncertainty while waiting for a match."That's five years of uncertainty, five years of being paralyzed, five years of not being able to grow," he said.Organ donation advocates say the need for donors continues across Florida and the United States.Gray noted that a single donor has the potential to save multiple lives and help many more patients through tissue donation."One donor is to save upwards of nine lives and to be able to heal another 75 lives," Gray said.Behind those numbers are people awaiting a second chance, he said."Let's all be heroes and save lives," Gray added.Advocates say organ donation often allows families to find meaning during some of life's most difficult moments."I would hope that they could see the lasting impact that a selfless act can make on others," Craft said. Many Americans say they’ve been confused or even fooled by political ads using artificial intelligence this campaign season, and want more rules governing how the technology is used, according to a new Scripps News/Talker Research poll.More than four-in-ten registered voters say they’ve seen something they thought was real in a political ad, only to later find it was AI-generated. Another 30% said they saw something they weren’t sure was real or AI.Some of the most talked about ads of the campaign have featured AI-generated candidates like Sen. Jon Ossoff in a beauty salon, James Talarico reciting old quotes out of context, and Sherrod Brown overstaying his welcome at a birthday party.More than half of survey respondents (56%) said they have seen Republicans using AI ads, compared with 49% saying they have seen ads for Democrats.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumorsAnd more than three-quarters of voters say there should be rules around how the technology is used in politics.In the absence of federal regulation, states have passed their own laws aimed at curbing the influence of AI or deepfakes in campaign advertising. Some states require disclosures or bar deepfake videos from being published in the weeks leading up to Election Day. But many of the regulations fail to keep up with the evolving use of what can be a cheap and effective new tool.An analysis from the Wesleyan Media Project from early September found AI tools had been used in at least 164 ads, 69% of which did not disclose AI was used. Eighty percent were from Republicans or Republican-leaning groups.Still, a similar amount of voters in both parties say there should be rules around how the technology is used, according to the Scripps News/Talker Research poll, including 77% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans.Concerns about how AI could impact areas outside politics also cut across party lines. Large swaths of the country worry about the impact AI could have on their jobs (61%), government institutions (83%), financial institutions (81%), and their physical safety (57%).Nearly 80% say they see content they believe was generated by AI at least once per day.This random double-opt-in online survey of 1,000 U.S. registered voters was commissioned by Scripps News and conducted by market research company Talker Research, in accordance with the Market Research Society’s code of conduct. Data was collected from Sept. The margin of error is +/- 2.2 points with 95% confidence

Republicans are spending hundreds of millions of dollars on advertising in battleground Senate races as they scramble to defend increasingly competitive GOP seats in the final stretch of the midterms.But when it comes to how far they can stretch a dollar, they’re effectively paying premium prices at Whole Foods while Democrats are shopping deals at Costco.RELATED STORY | Trump is heading all the way to Alaska in a sign of just how close its Senate race may beAcross nine of the most competitive Senate races last month, Republicans cumulatively outspent Democrats on broadcast TV ads by nearly 100% more, $233 million to $121 million, according to AdImpact data, but only saw about 40% more rating points.The disparity comes down to a difference in strategy. Republicans are relying heavily on outside groups, like super PACs, that pay elevated rates for ads and are making big buys late in the campaign, when inventory is stretched.By contrast, Democrats are taking advantage of discounted rates for candidates and earlier, less expensive reservations.At this stage in the game, Republicans are spending more to get less, which means the “shock and awe” of their massive dollar advantage isn’t necessarily translating to an actual impact on the ground, according to veteran Republican strategist John Thomas.A better metric, he said, is to consider the gross rating points, or GRPs, a unit advertisers use to measure the reach and frequency of an ad campaign, independent of how much was paid for it.In those nine races – where outside groups accounted for about 9 in 10 Republican ad dollars, compared to about half for Democrats – Democrats paid $201 per GRP, while Republicans paid about $274.In some races in September, Democrats actually outpaced Republicans in GRPs, completely overcoming their spending edge.In North Carolina, for example, Republicans outspent Democrats by about $17 million to $14 million on TV ads in September, as former Gov. Roy Cooper poses a major threat to former RNC Chair Michael Whatley and the GOP chances of holding Sen. But Democrats got more than 71,000 GRPs from their spend while Republicans got about 58,000. And at the beginning of October – recognizing the costly, difficult road ahead for Whatley – Republicans actually began cutting their remaining ad bookings by about $15 million.Democrats were also outspent last month by Republicans in Maine by about 32%, another premier battleground race where former state Sen. Troy Jackson is looking to unseat veteran GOP incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, who has received major backing from national Republicans. But here, again, despite being outspent, Democrats got 6% more GRPs for their money.Even in Texas – where Democrats were blasted by Republican ad money in September, outspent more than 4 times over – the GRP gap was proportionally much smaller. Republicans got only 2.6 times more GRPs.A GOP super PAC had to spend more than $22 million to air its top ad, touting Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s record as a prosecutor, about 15,500 times in September. Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico’s campaign spent a little under $4 million to air its most aired ad, casting Paxton as “the most corrupt politician in Texas,” about 8,000 times. That amounts to less than one-fifth the spending for about half the airtime.Lauren French, communications director for Senate Majority PAC, a leading Democratic super PAC, also emphasized that buying TV late in the cycle becomes exorbitantly expensive. “The nitty-gritty of campaigning is that not all ad space costs the same,” she said.“If you are buying something in February, it’s going to be a lot cheaper, and you’re going to get a lot more bang for your buck than, say, if you’re buying it in September. So that’s why you’re seeing this huge disconnect between what Republicans are paying and what Democrats are paying on average in some of these races,” French said.In seven of the top nine Senate races by total TV and radio ad spending in September, Democrats paid less per GRP than Republicans.The two exceptions were New Hampshire and Alaska. Confident in their nominees, Republicans were able to secure comparable or better rates in both states’ key markets. In New Hampshire, this was reinforced by Republicans allocating relatively more to cheaper secondary markets.“Broadly speaking, Republicans are using their money pretty ineffectively, and public polling is saying that people are not seeing their ads as much as one would expect. So, by that definition alone, some of their money is being set on fire. We are being outspent in a lot of these states, which means we have to make more strategic decisions,” French said.Thomas said that Texas, in particular, was emblematic of this effect, with GOP outside groups mounting an urgent rescue effort for Paxton and pouring money into the state. He noted that Paxton allies had taken to buying ad time on national NFL broadcasts because local markets had grown so crowded. That’s why people across the country are seeing Texas Senate ads in games that don’t include the Dallas Cowboys or Houston Texans.RELATED STORY | Barack Obama to campaign with Ohio Democrats as he expands his outreach ahead of Election Day“In some cases, because the commercial rate is so high in a local, like a Houston spot, it actually sometimes can be cheaper to buy a national spot,” he said.Democrats’ efficiency advantage might have been much greater, given their candidates have consistently raised more money their Republican opponents on a campaign-to-campaign basis, allowing them to spend more directly on their own ads at cheap rates.But thanks to a recent Supreme Court ruling, for the first time this year, national party committees can take advantage of candidate ad rates through coordinated buys.This means well-funded national committees like the National Republican Congressional Committee or National Republican Senate Committee can team up with candidates – like Mike Rogers in Michigan or Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio – and foot the bill for pricey ad campaigns while getting candidate discounts.The expansion of coordinated buying has allowed Republicans to blunt the Democratic candidate fundraising advantage. Democrats can do the same, but the GOP has taken to it far more aggressively: In September, GOP advertisers spent more than $30 million on coordinated ad buys, compared to about $5 million from Democrats.Outside groups like super PACs still play a dominant role, however, due to their unique ability to accept unlimited donations and make unlimited expenditures.“The money is actually very, very inefficient, but the benefit, even with the inefficiency of a super PAC, is one or two people can cut checks and fund the whole thing,” Thomas said.

Lucie Boulevard say more needs to be done to protect pedestrians as construction continues on the busy road. Their concerns come after a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student died from injuries he suffered when he was hit by an SUV while walking to school. Police say the freshman was walking along the edge of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on the morning of Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He was pronounced clinically deceased two days later. His family chose to donate his organs . Much of the roadway remains under construction, and there are no sidewalks along large sections of the corridor. Recent heavy rain also left portions of the shoulder flooded, further limiting space for pedestrians. "He was just going to school," said neighbor Irene Ange. "He was just starting his high school year. He had the right to be safe." Irene Ange, who has lived near the boulevard for more than two decades, says students often walk or bike close to traffic, sometimes before sunrise. The stretch of road is dangerous, Ange said. It’s very dark, and drivers are not following the speed limits. Ange said she saw first responders rushing to the crash site and was heartbroken for the student and his family. See also: Suspect booked into Martin County Jail after undercover drug sting, sheriff says The teen’s mother told CBS12 by phone that her son was a people person who made friends easily. She said the family does not want this to happen to another child. The Florida Department of Transportation is widening the southern portion of Port St. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four and adding sidewalks on both sides of the road. FDOT says the sidewalks will be eight to 10 feet wide. The project is expected to be completed in winter 2028, with an estimated cost of about $25.6 million. CBS 12 saw crews building sidewalks several blocks from where the crash happened. FDOT did not respond to questions about what pedestrian safety measures are in place while construction continues. "No accountability with that response because now there's another death," Ange said. Ange says more needs to be done now to keep children safe on their way to school. "This did not have to happen to this family," Ange said. The family now have to mourn him." The driver initially told officers he believed he had struck a construction barrel and has been cooperating with investigators. It remains unclear whether any charges will be filed.

Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Obtained 911 recordings capture the frantic moments following the crash. In one call, a person inside the Toyota pickup truck described the aftermath. "We got hit, and it's like, there's blood all over our car," the caller told a dispatcher. Another caller reported seeing the white van crash into the nearby building while trying to get away. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. According to a police news release, the driver ran northbound after crashing into the salon, located at 2508 Okeechobee Road. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:52 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. Police said the victim's identity had not yet been confirmed as of Monday, and confirmation was still pending before next of kin could be notified. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information about the crash or the driver's whereabouts is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or submit a tip through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers .

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives announced Friday it will no longer enforce National Firearms Act registration and approval requirements for suppressors, short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns.The move eliminates what was often a months-long process that required buyers to obtain federal approval, register the items with the government and pay a tax stamp before taking possession. Federal background checks are still required.For firearm retailers in West Palm Beach, the change is already having an impact.At We Kick Brass, owner Mike Perez said customers previously had to navigate a lengthy approval process to legally purchase suppressors and certain firearms regulated under the National Firearms Act."People were legally able to own these firearms," Perez said. "They just had to wait a longer process. It had to get ATF approval."For decades, suppressors and short-barreled rifles and shotguns were subject to National Firearms Act requirements that included registration, federal approval and a tax stamp.The ATF announced Friday it will no longer enforce those requirements for those items.The move follows a federal court ruling in Texas involving National Firearms Act registration requirements and comes after Congress reduced the tax stamp fee from $200 to zero.Perez said the biggest change is the amount of paperwork buyers no longer have to complete."The biggest change is less paperwork," Perez said. "It's a lot easier for someone to come in here and purchase a firearm and feel safe about it and secure about it."He said some customers who once faced waits stretching nine months, 14 months or longer may now be able to take possession much sooner."They no longer have to wait 14 months, or nine months, or even more than a day if they have a concealed weapon firearm permit," Perez said. "They can leave with that same day and start training immediately and empower themselves and be able to protect themselves or their family."Perez said interest surged almost immediately after the federal announcement.When WPTV's Michael Hoffman visited We Kick Brass, several customers were at the shop picking up suppressors.Perez believes the changes will make firearms and accessories that were already legal to own more accessible to law-abiding buyers.Perez also has personal experience with short-barreled rifles. In 2018, he was involved in a self-defense shooting in which he used one."I used a short-barreled rifle to save my mother's life," Perez said. "They are just simply put the best and most effective tools."Asked what could happen if a future administration attempted to reverse the policy, Perez said he believes current owners would likely be protected."I imagine that they would be grandfathered in," Perez said. "You can't make millions of Americans felons overnight by the flick of a pen. It just makes no sense."The ATF's policy change does not eliminate all National Firearms Act regulations.Machine guns and destructive devices, including bombs, rockets and grenades, remain subject to federal requirements.Customers purchasing firearms must also continue to undergo background checks and comply with all applicable federal and state laws.For those concerned about expanded access to suppressors and short-barreled firearms, Perez said the changes affect law-abiding citizens."We are just allowing people, law-abiding citizens, the ability to protect themselves with the right firearm to do so," Perez said.Florida gun owners should also be aware that state law prohibits short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns unless they are lawfully owned under federal law. The ATF has said it cannot provide guidance on whether an unregistered firearm would satisfy that requirement under Florida law.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A 54-year-old man suspected of robbing a pizza delivery driver was fatally shot by a Palm Beach County sheriff's deputy Tuesday after a pursuit ended near Jog and Woolbright roads, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said.Bradshaw said the investigation began after a pizza delivery driver was robbed around 10 p.m. The suspect allegedly ordered a pizza to a Lake Worth location and told the driver he only had a $100 bill. When the driver pulled out money to make change, the suspect allegedly grabbed him, and the two struggled over the cash.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The delivery driver provided investigators with a description of the suspect's vehicle and a license plate number, Bradshaw said.Investigators entered that information into license plate readers and received an alert Tuesday that the vehicle was in the Lake Park area.PBSO tactical units located the vehicle and conducted surveillance to confirm the registered owner was driving, according to Bradshaw. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.BREAKING NEWS: Deputy fatally shoots robbery suspect after chaseA PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said. Something was wrapped around his right hand, and deputies in the helicopter believed he might have been holding a firearm.Bradshaw said the man attempted to take cover behind concrete light poles as deputies tried to stop him using two types of less-lethal weapons. Three less-lethal rounds struck him but had no effect, according to the sheriff.Bradshaw said the man repeatedly yelled at deputies, "You're gonna have to kill me."When the man reached a second pole, Bradshaw said he got into a kneeling position and raised his hands in what appeared to be a shooting position.A deputy then opened fire, striking the man. Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for projects along the Southern Grove, a developing jobs corridor in the city. One of those plans: the long-awaited Costco retail store. “This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time,” Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the 163,000-square-foot store is just the beginning for a new phase of growth in western Port St. “This is getting closer to the finish line,” Samples said. The Costco will join other companies like Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers, calling the Southern Grove area home. McCurry said since the jobs are now here, new commercial development will follow. “They see all the development that’s occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see,” said McCurry. “It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here.” City council approved two other major site plans for the area, including a 5.5-acre site making up the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District set to bring restaurants and retail. “This area has historically been largely underserved by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities,” McCurry said. “It’s kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there’s more to come.” The other plan is space for an acute care rehabilitation hospital, featuring inpatient and outpatient services with 42 beds in a more than 55,000-square-foot building. “A growing area needs services, and that’s just another component of services that are coming into the area is expanded healthcare access,” McCurry said. McCurry said the plans for retail, healthcare and entertainment are fulfilling the city’s master plan for what Southern Grove was destined to become. “The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together. What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen,” McCurry said. Samples said Costco still must close on the land, move on to construction design planning and permitting before any shovels hit the ground.

Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday unanimously to move forward with a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities.Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi explained it's "an opportunity to say, 'pause,' let's hear from people, let’s have the opportunity for experts to come and speak to us on both sides.”Watch report from Cassandra Garcia:Commissioners explained they would consider extending the moratorium later if they need more time.“If it takes a year, a year and a half, two years, whatever it takes, whatever it takes, we should be doing this,” said Martin County Commissioner Eileen Vargas.Tuesday's vote marked the first of two hearings scheduled this month on the proposed moratorium.PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Martin County eyes pause on data center developmentCommissioners are expected to revisit the issue on Oct. 27, when another vote will be required.Residents are now hoping the county will use the time to consider their concerns.“For me it’s wildlife so these areas are in largely rural or large plots of land and so you take that area and develop it and these facilities are massive—millions and millions of square feet, no animals can live there anymore, or the hum is going to affect the animals,” said Sergei Kelley, who spoke at the meeting.Martin County resident Scott Butler added, "The fear of the use of all this water we have [...] and understanding what these data center[s] are going to use.”The discussion comes as Martin County has already received an application for a data center. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership, the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters.More than 74% of firefighters who participated in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said they had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, while 97% said the same of district attorney Kim Sabol.WATCH BELOW: St. Lucie County fire chief faces calls to resign after no-confidence vote"I think it's a wake-up call," Fire Board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner James Clasby told WPTV Investigates. "They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action." When investigative reporter Kate Hussey asked whether he believed that action should include Lee's resignation, Clasby said yes."I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.The vote is the latest fallout from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A.A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing. One showed firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees.Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation.The three have maintained the activity was consensual and "all in good fun.""It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson previously told WPTV."We're all still friends," Boudrias said.Their terminations sparked pushback from firefighters and members of the community, which eventually led to the union's no-confidence vote."The amount that voted no confidence really sends a message that we have, in their opinion, a lack of confidence in their leadership," union representative Ryan Sapp said.Sapp is representing the three firefighters in their fight for reinstatement. With previous settlement offers now off the table, Sapp said he recently met with Lee and district leadership to ask how they planned to respond to the vote."His response was that he doesn't feel a change in leadership would change the confidence issue or the morale," Sapp said.The vote comes as the district is already undergoing changes in leadership.Sabol has submitted notice of her retirement, effective in December. Meanwhile, a reassignment notice obtained by WPTV Investigates shows Gonzalez is being moved from assistant chief to battalion chief.Clasby questioned the decision, particularly given the no-confidence vote against Gonzalez."I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," Clasby said.The district told WPTV that Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and said the move had been under discussion "for some time prior to recent events."In a statement, the district said it "recognizes" the results of the no-confidence vote and the importance of listening to its personnel.The district said it remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking "appropriate action" to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters.Sapp said rebuilding that trust could prove difficult."I think it's hard whenever you see those staggering numbers, that lack confidence in leadership, to rebound it back," he said.The Fire Board is also weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin while working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled.That work is expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting.Sapp said their last settlement offer, an offer to reinstate the three firefighters with a three-shift suspension, was not accepted. "I do want to say, this is a great department," Sapp added. We have great men and women that work here. In light of all this bad publicity we've had, I promise you these members, these employees that I have, they genuinely enjoy serving this community and do the absolute best they can do."
