Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Obtained 911 recordings capture the frantic moments following the crash. In one call, a person inside the Toyota pickup truck described the aftermath. "We got hit, and it's like, there's blood all over our car," the caller told a dispatcher. Another caller reported seeing the white van crash into the nearby building while trying to get away. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. According to a police news release, the driver ran northbound after crashing into the salon, located at 2508 Okeechobee Road. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:52 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. Police said the victim's identity had not yet been confirmed as of Monday, and confirmation was still pending before next of kin could be notified. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information about the crash or the driver's whereabouts is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or submit a tip through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers .

Just days after MARTY public bus services abruptly shut down in Martin County, county commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to allow the county administrator to negotiate a new contract with a company that could restore service. The vote gives county administration the green light to begin negotiations with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county’s public bus system. For former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence, Tuesday’s decision offered a sign of hope after he and several other drivers suddenly lost their jobs last Thursday. “I’m hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work,” Lawrence said. Lawrence was among the drivers impacted when Martin County Transit LLC, the company previously operating MARTY, abruptly stopped services last Thursday. The company cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as reasons for its decision to discontinue service. During Tuesday’s county commission meeting, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton explained that county officials had spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. “We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us,” Gorton said. According to Gorton, the county evaluated several proposals before identifying MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county’s emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million. Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously to end their lease with the former operator of Crabby's Dockside and begin searching for a new operator for the waterfront restaurant. The restaurant, located along Avenue A at the Fort Pierce Marina, closed in February. The city said its operator, Winking Starfish, owed more than $418,000 in rent, taxes, and late fees. After recalculating the balance, the city now says the amount owed is nearly $334,000. Winking Starfish identified a potential new operator for the restaurant, but city officials said the proposal sought favorable terms. City Manager Richard Chess told commissioners that the city would allow interested restaurateurs to compete for the location. The city plans to set requirements for potential operators, with the city commission making the final decision. "Our marina is very, very successful, and we're very proud of it, and that location, that Crabby's location, is a very critical part of the marina," Mayor Linda Hudson said. Chess also said during the meeting that a new agreement would combine rent and other payments into one amount, based on the property's market value. Local leaders joined housing advocates in West Palm Beach on Tuesday to discuss rising homeowners association fees and condo assessments that they say are putting financial pressure on residents, particularly seniors and people struggling to remain in their homes.WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach County leaders tackle rising HOA feesThe panel, organized by U.S. Lois Frankel, focused on potential solutions including more financial assistance for seniors, greater state oversight of homeowners associations and limits on attorney fees charged to condo owners."This is really tough," state Sen. "But we don’t want another Surfside, but at the same time what we want to do is create new affordable housing."Florida condominium owners have faced increased financial pressures following reforms adopted in response to the 2021 Surfside condominium collapse. The reforms included inspection and reserve requirements intended to address building safety.The discussion comes as Florida communities rank among those with the nation's highest HOA burdens. A Realtor.com analysis previously covered by WPTV found seven of the nation's 10 metro areas with the highest HOA fees relative to estimated mortgage payments were in Florida. Lucie ranked fifth, while the Sebastian-Vero Beach area ranked ninth.Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said questions about transparency are adding to homeowners' concerns."What we're seeing is a lot of transparency issues, questioning each other, are these fees necessary or not necessary," Flores said.Panelists also discussed reports of condo owners being forced from their homes as association costs become unaffordable.Among the potential solutions raised Tuesday were additional financial assistance for seniors and more state oversight of HOAs.Flores said keeping seniors in their homes should be part of the discussion."More dollars coming to help these seniors stay in their homes because if they don’t stay in their homes we have to find another solution of where will they go to live," Flores said.The panel also discussed controlling attorney fees charged to condo owners.For Florida homeowners, the issue goes beyond association dues. Rising HOA fees can add to other major housing expenses, including property taxes and insurance. Tuesday's discussion highlighted the challenge facing policymakers: ensuring condominium buildings have the money needed to address safety concerns while finding ways to prevent those costs from pricing residents out of their homes.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. WPTV has been reporting extensively on the growth at the Vero Beach Regional Airport when it comes to flights.But on Tuesday, Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the airport."We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years,” Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience."Dembeck took WPTV to the site, which sits just outside the gates of the terminal along Aviation Boulevard."They're going to have a hotel right next door that they can come, they can stay, wait for their flight, and then go right over to the terminal."But the lodging is more than just for passengers.Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the hotel could attract more businesses to the city of Vero Beach and beyond."The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes,” said Cartland. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."While the hotel is close to the airport, Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the developer of the project, said one big need for the extra lodging is just down the street at the Jackie Robinson Training Complex."We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball,” Maxey said.Maxey said the hotel will also feature a “homerun dugout amenity” for families."Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the major league baseball players,” Maxey said.Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and expected to be completed by end of 2028.

Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say fled after a crash that killed a motorcyclist Sunday night.The crash happened around 8:52 p.m. near South 25th Street and Okeechobee Road. Officers responded after receiving multiple 911 calls about a crash involving a motorcycle.According to preliminary information from the Fort Pierce Police Department, a white box van traveling east on Okeechobee Road struck a blue motorcycle and attempted to leave the scene.Police said the van's driver made a U-turn in the eastbound lanes while fleeing, crossed the westbound lanes and crashed into Kings and Queens Unisex Salon at 2508 Okeechobee Road.The driver then got out of the van and fled north on foot, police said.When officers arrived, they found the motorcyclist in the outside eastbound lane of Okeechobee Road and determined the person had died. Lucie County Fire Rescue also responded.The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office K-9 and Aviation units assisted Fort Pierce police in searching for the driver, but police said he had not been located as of Monday. Two other vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene.Police described the driver as an adult Hispanic man wearing a dark-colored top and light-colored pants or shorts.The identity of the person killed has not been confirmed.The Fort Pierce Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit and Crime Scene Investigations are investigating.Anyone with information about the crash or the driver's identity or whereabouts is asked to contact Fort Pierce police at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

A nurse at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie is under investigation after allegedly stealing fentanyl from a critically ill patient’s IV bag on June 24 and 25, according to police. "They did an internal investigation where the Department of Health was then notified, in turn notifying PSLPD where we started our investigation in early August," said Officer Brittany McNally, public information officer for the Port St. Police said a family member of the patient reported seeing 54-year-old Leslie Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient’s fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket, and leave the room. "That’s not standard procedure, from what I understand at the hospital," McNally said. "But again, she’s not even assigned that patient. And there was no initial justification for her to even be in that room at the time." Investigators said Pope returned the following evening and approached the IV equipment again, but the family member intervened and stopped her. Hospital video reportedly showed Pope manipulating protective caps on the IV equipment, but investigators said she did not remove any fluid during the second incident. And this individual had this monitor that had video recordings, which was a key piece of evidence in this case and completely contradicted what her recollection was," McNally said. Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for projects along the Southern Grove, a developing jobs corridor in the city.One of those plans: the long-awaited Costco retail store.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie City Council approves site plan for Costco"This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time,” Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said.Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the 163,000-square-foot store is just the beginning for a new phase of growth in western Port St. Lucie."This is getting closer to the finish line," Samples said.The Costco will join other companies like Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers, calling the Southern Grove area home.McCurry said since the jobs are now here, new commercial development will follow."They see all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see,” said McCurry. A Florida prisoner who said he killed his cellmate specifically to get on death row was executed Tuesday, nearly 18 years after the attack.James Robertson, 63, declined to offer any last words before receiving a three-drug injection and was pronounced dead about 10 minutes later. It was a stark contrast to the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee two weeks ago, where she was rushed to the hospital after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Robertson’s execution, the first in Florida since Pike, comes at a time of escalating attention on the death penalty in the United States. The Pentagon said last week that it would livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, drawing criticism from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers.“Florida has a sound lethal injection process and protocol,” Jordan Kirkland, a state Department of Corrections spokesperson, said at a news conference before the execution. Although he couldn’t speak to Tennessee’s lethal injection procedure, he said Florida would make sure its process was “humane and dignified.”Florida executes people by injecting them with a sedative, a paralytic, and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.Robertson had pleaded guilty to first-degree murder for strangling Frank Hart while he slept in 2008, and waived all appeals. He told investigators that he did it so he wouldn't have to live out his days in prison.Hart was killed just eight days before he was due to be released, his daughter, Rebecca Hart, told reporters at Florida State Prison. She stressed that her father was not just a piece of Robertson’s story.“When someone you love is taken from you in such a violent way, the world keeps moving, even when a part of yours feels like it has stopped,” she read. “Other people go on with their lives, but you carry your loss into every tomorrow.”Robertson was 17 years old when he went to prison in 1980 for burglary and assault. Years of convictions for escape, battery and weapons while in prison kept adding time to his total sentence. Hart had been sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction.Robertson was supposed to be one of two executions carried out by Florida on Tuesday, but Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant last week for William Lee Thompson. The Republican governor did not provide a reason but had temporarily stayed the execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation.Records show this was the first time DeSantis withdrew a death warrant. Thompson, 74, will remain on death row, and a new death warrant could be signed in the future. His attorneys say he has dementia and failing health, and they want him transferred to a medical facility.DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson. Bob Graham and Bob Martinez both scheduled executions for Thompson in the 1980s, but years of appeals and stays allowed him to avoid the electric chair, the state's method of execution at the time.Thompson was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester.DeSantis oversaw 19 executions in 2025, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Robertson was the state’s 17th execution of 2026, with two more already scheduled, not counting Thompson.DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has made few public comments about the unprecedented number of executions but explained previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed on Oct. 20, followed by Jesse Guardado, 64, on Nov. Reaves was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy after dropping a gun in front of the law enforcement officer in 1986. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.

By: Scott Sutton Posted BOCA RATON, Fla. — The Boca Raton Community Redevelopment Agency has approved a proposal for a private social and wellness club near Sanborn Square. The eight-story project would bring restaurants, wellness centers and major redevelopment to the area. The proposal comes as multiple major projects are reshaping the downtown corridor, including the Aletto mixed-use development and the previously approved Mizner Plaza hotel project. Supporters say the club could bring new customers and tax revenue to the area, while some residents worry about increased traffic, parking demand and what they consider overdevelopment.

A $43 million expansion project to level up the Port of Palm Beach is moving forward, with port leaders saying the improvements could attract new cruise opportunities, boost tourism and generate more economic activity in Palm Beach County.But some residents are urging local leaders to slow down and take a closer look at what those changes could mean for the waters around Peanut Island and the Inlet.WATCH BELOW: $43M Port of Palm Beach expansion raises concernsLast month, the Port Commission voted to seek proposals for a project that would expand cruise facilities, a plan identified as a priority in the port's 2023 master plan. The project includes a parking garage, a new passenger loading bridge, expanded screening and baggage areas and the addition of mooring dolphins that would allow the port to accommodate longer ships."Our goal is to bring more cruise passengers to Palm Beach County and the City of Riviera Beach, creating greater economic benefits to our community," said Blair Ciklin, chair of the Port Commission.According to the port, there is currently one cruise ship homeported in Palm Beach County, the Margaritaville at Sea Paradise, which began operating from the port in 2022.For Bradford Gary, a longtime mariner and Palm Beach resident, the concern is not cruise ships themselves."I don't want to stop the port from development, but I don't want them to put a big boat in here that's going to hazard small boats and swimmers and mariners," Gary said.Gary emailed WPTV reporter Joel Lopez, worried that larger vessels could create conflicts with the recreational users who frequent Peanut Island and surrounding waters.He appeared before the Town of Palm Beach council on Tuesday urging local leaders to support federal restrictions that would cap ships entering the Port of Palm Beach at roughly 700 feet in length, about the size of the Margaritaville at Sea Paradise currently operating from the port."We don't think those big 700-foot, 1,000-foot boats mix with small boats or swimmers or traffic, particularly on Peanut Island," he said.Lopez took Gary's concerns straight to Port of Palm Beach officials for answers on safety and impacts to the waterways."So right now we fit our ship, which is 730 (feet), but it's really not about the size of the vessel. It's about the controls of the vessel," said Michael Meekins, executive director of the Port of Palm Beach.Meekins said newer ships can come equipped with advanced propulsion systems that make them easier to maneuver than traditional vessels.The debate also centers on proposed mooring dolphins, offshore structures that allow ships to tie up beyond the existing dock.Meekins described the structures as a common maritime tool that can accommodate different vessel configurations without constructing an entirely new dock."You have the normal pier and then out from the pier you just have a catwalk, and then there's a concrete anchorage system with some moorings on it, and that allows the ship to tie up out there without having to build an entire dock," Meekins said.He said no final approval has been made on how many mooring dolphins will be installed or how far out from the port they will be.I addressed Gary's concerns about larger ships with boaters, swimmers and snorkelers near Peanut Island, and Meekins pushed back."The cruise line really has zero impact on the local tourists who are going out to Peanut Island or anything else," Meekins said. "All it does is open up and vary the different options that the port has to offer."According to Meekins, cruise ships typically arrive before most beachgoers and snorkelers head out for the day and depart around dusk. He also noted the port currently has only one cruise berth, limiting the amount of cruise traffic moving through the inlet.Beyond cruise operations, Meekins says the project is intended to improve the passenger experience and create opportunities for future growth."It's a magnificent job producer, and it creates a lot of economic impact to the local community," he said.The port says cruise activity currently accounts for about 30% of its revenue and supports jobs ranging from vessel services and maintenance to hotels, restaurants and transportation providers throughout the region.Meekins said the Port of Palm Beach District has not levied property taxes since 1975.Design and permitting work is expected to begin following the solicitation process. According to Meekins, renderings could become available in the coming months, while construction is likely still several years away.Meanwhile, Gary says he hopes the discussion continues before final decisions are made.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A 54-year-old man suspected of robbing a pizza delivery driver was fatally shot by a Palm Beach County sheriff's deputy Tuesday after a pursuit ended near Jog and Woolbright roads, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said.Bradshaw said the investigation began after a pizza delivery driver was robbed around 10 p.m. The suspect allegedly ordered a pizza to a location and told the driver he only had a $100 bill. When the driver pulled out money to make change, the suspect allegedly grabbed him, and the two struggled over the cash.BREAKING NEWS: Deputy fatally shoots robbery suspect after chaseThe delivery driver provided investigators with a description of the suspect's vehicle and a license plate number, Bradshaw said.Investigators entered that information into license plate readers and received an alert Tuesday that the vehicle was in the Lake Park area.PBSO tactical units located the vehicle and conducted surveillance to confirm the registered owner was driving, according to Bradshaw. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.A PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said. Something was wrapped around his right hand, and deputies in the helicopter believed he might have been holding a firearm.Bradshaw said the man attempted to take cover behind concrete light poles as deputies tried to stop him using two types of less-lethal weapons. Three less-lethal rounds struck him but had no effect, according to the sheriff.Bradshaw said the man repeatedly yelled at deputies, "You're gonna have to kill me."When the man reached a second pole, Bradshaw said he got into a kneeling position and raised his hands in what appeared to be a shooting position.A deputy then opened fire, striking the man. He died at the scene.Bradshaw later confirmed investigators did not find a firearm on the man.The sheriff said the 54-year-old was a convicted felon whose criminal history included carjacking, robbery, kidnapping, assault and drug offenses.The man's identity has not been released pending notification of his next of kin.Jog Road was shut down in both directions between Woolbright Road and Grand Isle Drive during the investigation.Bradshaw said additional information, including a more detailed timeline and information about the suspect, will be released as the investigation continues.This is a developing story.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Tuesday that 25 people have been charged in connection with what authorities describe as a large-scale drug trafficking organization responsible for distributing cocaine, fentanyl and methamphetamine across multiple Florida counties.According to investigators, 19 suspects are already in custody and six remain outstanding following a months-long investigation dubbed Operation Ice Breaker.WATCH BELOW: 25 charged in major drug trafficking investigationOfficials said the investigation targeted a drug trafficking network operating mainly in Palm Beach, Broward and St. Lucie counties, as well as communities in Miami-Dade and Florida's west coast."These were not users. These were wholesalers," Uthmeier said during a news conference in Boynton Beach "These were large-scale traffickers pushing massive amounts of drugs through our communities."The investigation began in March 2026 and involved the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Office of Statewide Prosecution.Authorities identified Ariel Fernandez Alonso as the primary target of the investigation. Through undercover work and other investigative efforts, agents established probable cause to charge 25 individuals and obtained 21 search warrants, which were served over the past several days.As a result of the operation, investigators said they seized:Approximately 45.5 kilograms of cocaine84 grams of fentanylAbout 2.5 pounds of methamphetaminePrescription pills14 pounds of marijuanaFive rifles11 handguns, including one reported stolenOfficials said several of the suspects face charges including conspiracy to commit racketeering, drug trafficking and unlawful use of a two-way communications device. Uthmeier said some defendants face mandatory minimum prison sentences of 15 years if convicted.Investigators found evidence that large quantities of cocaine were being shipped into Florida from California, with some loads arriving weekly before being distributed throughout South Florida."When you've got investigators finding 20, 30, 40 kilos coming in every single week of cocaine, this is not just a small quantity hand-off," Uthmeier said. "This is a large-scale coordinated network that's passing through massive amounts of drugs."Major Lawrence Poston of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the arrests demonstrate the impact of coordinated law enforcement efforts."When we all combine our efforts together, we can take dangerous, violent individuals like this off the streets," Poston said.FDLE Special Agent in Charge Michael Stein highlighted the role of Florida's State Assistance for Fentanyl Eradication, or SAFE, program, which provides funding and resources for narcotics investigations.According to Stein, since the program was established in 2023, Florida law enforcement agencies have seized nearly 300 kilograms of fentanyl, more than 400 kilograms of cocaine and more than 200 kilograms of methamphetamine. Authorities have also confiscated more than $6 million in cash and over 1,000 firearms while making more than 3,000 arrests.Representatives from the Health Care District of Palm Beach County said local treatment and recovery programs have helped connect thousands of overdose patients with long-term care and support services.Uthmeier said the investigation remains active and additional charges could be filed as authorities continue to follow leads connected to the trafficking network."Our belief is that we've taken down the hub of the operation here in Florida," Uthmeier said. "We'll continue to follow the breadcrumbs and make additional arrests as needed."

South Florida utility crews and first responders are aiding recovery efforts in Florida's Panhandle following Hurricane Isaias. On Saturday, the Fort Pierce Utilities Authority sent seven crew members and five trucks to the area to help restore power. The crew is working with Choctawhatchee Electric Cooperative, also known as CHELCO, alongside other utility companies from across Florida. They are rebuilding power lines, removing damaged equipment, and installing new transformers and distribution lines. The American Public Power Association said nearly 67,000 CHELCO customers lost power during the storm, affecting about 90% of its system. Fort Pierce Utilities said a statewide mutual-aid agreement allows utilities to quickly send crews to areas where they are most needed. This agreement has also brought outside crews to South Florida following previous hurricanes. "Because of the collaboration and the help provided by the mutual aid agreements, we're able to help each other out. And we couldn't do it on our own. It's too much damage, and it gets our customers back up in a shorter amount of time when there's power loss," said Keith Stephens, director of gas and electric for Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. The Fort Pierce crew is expected to remain in the Panhandle throughout this week or as long as the crew's assistance is required. Florida Power Light has also sent thousands of lineworkers to the Gulf Coast to help restore power. Palm Beach County Fire Rescue and Delray Beach Fire Rescue have deployed crews as well, and they are expected to assist with recovery efforts for the next two weeks.

Lynora's Italian restaurant, a South Florida staple that started as an 800-square-foot pizzeria in Lake Worth in 1976, is marking 50 years in business — and the family behind it is planning to grow beyond Palm Beach County.Angelo Abbenante, son of founders Raffaele and Maria Abbenante, now leads the restaurant brand, which currently has 6 locations spanning Palm Beach County from Jupiter to Boca Raton."From a little hole in the wall in Lake Worth to now we've gotten to the point where we have six locations we have about five more in the pipeline," he said.The expansion will reach beyond Palm Beach County, with Melbourne set to be next."Our next location is going to be Melbourne, Florida and then from there we're going to hit Fort Lauderdale, and then we have Wellington, Royal Palm Beach coming and then Delray," Abbenante said.The Lynora's story begins with Abbenante's parents, who emigrated from Italy and chose South Florida after his mother found the cold weather in New York unbearable."They came to Italy first and stopped in New York and my mom didn't like the cold weather so she decided to go back to Italy or move to a warmer area, so they had the opportunity to come to South Florida and they landed in Lake Worth," he said.Growing up in the family business meant no traditional weekends off."We didn't have the luxury of the typical American weekends off, this was 7 days a week, 24 hours a day, it was really just putting their feet in the ground. Working 7 days a week and really trying to build a great life for the family," Abbenante said.He worked his way through every job in the restaurant."Dishwashing, washing tables, bartending, making pizzas, working with my mom in the line, just doing whatever had to be done," Abbenante said.I reviewed an original menu, a reminder of how it all began. A large pizza was priced at $3.65 to $4.70. Many of those early dishes are still on the menu today."Yeah, we have all the same dishes from our hoagies where we use the same bread to our eggplant parmesan to our chicken and veal parmesan," Abbenante said.Reflecting on 50 years, Abbenante said family unity and commitment to quality are what have set Lynora's apart."We didn't go out on weekends you know me and my brother it was like we were working and helping mom and helping Dad and when you get to that point you think about the business a little differently - we are really united and I think that is what has made Lynora's so special for the last 50 years. Is when you walk into these restaurants…you get that energy and you get that homemade food. And everything is made with love so it's been a great run and we're looking forward to the next 50 years," Abbenante said.The recipes have remained true to their origins, with bread, pasta, and sauces still made in-house."It really brings us back to how it all started right and the food has been the same, we still make our own bread we still make our own pasta and all the dishes we have created have really been from our mom the sauces," Abbenante said.Among Lynora's most distinctive preparations is its signature sauce."One of the things that is really true to us is how our sauces are made our sauces still take 8 hours to make," Abbenante said.The restaurant's famous meatballs carry the same recipes as when Lynora's first opened."These are actually the same recipes that my mom started 50 years ago, you can kind of see our sauce is a little different than most restaurants... our flavors are basically built into the sauce and our meatballs you know they really speak for themselves," Abbenante said.Quality and consistency, Abbenante says, are the foundation of the restaurant's longevity."It's about making sure that we have the quality ingredients, highest quality, and when you make the food - you have to make sure it's done consistent year in and year out, day in and day out, and when you do that, that's the secret sauce," Abbenante said.Each Lynora's location is designed to reflect the personality of its community."So, when you're Jupiter you get that little feel of Jupiter and when you're in Boca you get that feel of Boca," Abbenante said.Lynora's pizza is made in a wood-burning oven using a hybrid style that blends New York and classic Italian techniques."So we do a mixture of New York style and classic Napoletano pizza and so it's a hybrid and the reason we do that is, because of our oven - our oven is not a gas oven it's a wood burning oven," Abbenante said. "We cook our pizzas typically between 700 to 800 degrees."During a demonstration, Abbenante chose his personal favorite to make."So, we're going to make my favorite which is a classic it's Margherita," he said.Community support, Abbenante says, has been a key ingredient in the restaurant's success."Without the community giving us the support we have we wouldn't be where we're at," he said.As Lynora's enters its next chapter, Abbenante says what it takes has never changed."At the end of the day it's a lot of work a lot of sacrifice it's all the little things it's very meticulous and you have to love it. At the end of the day," he said.Watch "Finding Florida" each Sunday at 10 a.m. on WPTV!This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

For many working families in Palm Beach County, having a job is no longer enough to guarantee they can afford a place to live.That was the message from faith leaders and community members with People Engaged in Active Community Efforts (PEACE), who gathered Monday at St. Ann Catholic Church to call attention to the county’s housing affordability crisis and urge local leaders to take action.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:“We are gathered today because across our congregations and our community, we continue to hear the same concern,” said the Rev. Latifah Griffin, a PEACE board of trustees member. “People who are working here are struggling to live here.”PEACE is a coalition of 31 congregations across Palm Beach County. Members say conversations within their congregations reveal a growing number of residents struggling with rising rents, stagnant wages and the possibility of being priced out of the communities where they work and raise their families.Palm Beach County data underscores those concerns. According to the county’s January 2025 affordable housing report, the average rent for a two-bedroom apartment increased from $1,899 in 2021 to $2,833 in 2024 — a 49.2% increase in three years. The cost of buying a home has also risen. The county report found the median price of a single-family home climbed from $425,000 in late 2020 to $600,000 in late 2024, an increase of 41.2%. Nationally, Redfin reported in August 2026 that households needed an annual income of nearly $110,000 to afford a typical U.S. For residents working in service and other modest-wage jobs, those costs can make independent living difficult even when they work consistently.Harry Wolin shared his family's experience at Monday’s gathering. He said he and his wife, who are retired and living on a fixed income, help support their adult daughter, a waitress who lives in Lake Worth.Woolen said his daughter has worked in the restaurant industry for more than 20 years, but her income is not enough to afford housing without help from her parents.“She’s doing everything that we’ve told people they’re supposed to do: get a job, work hard, help support your family,” Wolin said. “And it just doesn’t work given the price of housing.”He said he worries about workers in similar circumstances who do not have relatives able to help them financially.“What do they do if they don’t have a family who can help them?” Wolin asked.Wolin said his family is willing to make sacrifices to ensure his daughter has a safe place to live, but he worries about what will happen when he and his wife are no longer able to provide that support.Mamie Kisner, who represents Tabernacle Missionary Baptist Church, said the experiences Wolin described reflect what PEACE members hear from families across the county.She said residents have reported increasing rents, adult children unable to afford homes of their own and families doubling up in crowded living conditions. Some workers are moving farther away in search of more affordable housing, she said, while businesses struggle to retain employees who cannot afford to live nearby.“These aren’t just numbers; these are people that we know and love,” Kisner said. Faith leaders urged elected officials to listen to residents experiencing housing insecurity and consider solutions that help working people remain in Palm Beach County.PEACE members said raising awareness is only one part of their effort. The organization is also encouraging residents to hear directly from county commission candidates about their understanding of the housing crisis and the steps they would take to address it.The group announced a community kickoff and Palm Beach County Commission candidate forum focused on affordable housing.The event is scheduled for Monday, Oct. Juliana Catholic Church.For PEACE members, the issue comes down to whether people who contribute to the county every day can afford to remain part of the communities they help sustain.

A 54-year-old man suspected of robbing a pizza delivery driver was fatally shot by a Palm Beach County sheriff's deputy Tuesday after a pursuit ended near Jog and Woolbright roads, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said.Bradshaw said the investigation began after a pizza delivery driver was robbed around 10 p.m. The suspect allegedly ordered a pizza to a location and told the driver he only had a $100 bill. When the driver pulled out money to make change, the suspect allegedly grabbed him, and the two struggled over the cash.The delivery driver provided investigators with a description of the suspect's vehicle and a license plate number, Bradshaw said.Investigators entered that information into license plate readers and received an alert Tuesday that the vehicle was in the Lake Park area.PBSO tactical units located the vehicle and conducted surveillance to confirm the registered owner was driving, according to Bradshaw. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.BREAKING NEWS: Jog Road shut down between Woolbright Road, Grand Isle DriveA PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said. Something was wrapped around his right hand, and deputies in the helicopter believed he might have been holding a firearm.Bradshaw said the man attempted to take cover behind concrete light poles as deputies tried to stop him using two types of less-lethal weapons. Three less-lethal rounds struck him but had no effect, according to the sheriff.Bradshaw said the man repeatedly yelled at deputies, "You're gonna have to kill me."When the man reached a second pole, Bradshaw said he got into a kneeling position and raised his hands in what appeared to be a shooting position.A deputy then opened fire, striking the man. He died at the scene.Bradshaw later confirmed investigators did not find a firearm on the man.The sheriff said the 54-year-old was a convicted felon whose criminal history included carjacking, robbery, kidnapping, assault and drug offenses.The man's identity has not been released pending notification of his next of kin.Jog Road was shut down in both directions between Woolbright Road and Grand Isle Drive during the investigation.Bradshaw said additional information, including a more detailed timeline and information about the suspect, will be released as the investigation continues.This is a developing story.

A legal battle has erupted in Martin County as the developer behind a massive data center project files a sprawling lawsuit against the Village of Indiantown, its village council, planning board, and local residents. Silver Fox 606 LLC filed the complaint and verified petition for a writ of prohibition, claiming local officials are illegally derailing its $25 million project. Silver Fox purchased the over 600-acre property at 13820 SW Silver Fox Lane in 2025 following zoning verifications confirming that computer and data processing facilities were permitted as an as-of-right use in Heavy Industrial districts. Following the 2026 municipal elections, a newly sworn-in village council attempted to stall or ban data center developments despite what the lawsuit alleges were prior municipal marketing efforts that actively recruited similar tech infrastructure. See also: ICU nurse accused of taking fentanyl from critically ill patient at PSL hospital Indiantown's Community and Economic Development Director administratively approved the Silver Fox plat on September 17. The lawsuit highlights a turbulent political climate, pointing to a September 1 emergency council meeting where the village manager and long-serving village attorney were ousted. Shortly after, an administrative appeal was filed by a local resident seeking to overturn the director's approvals. Silver Fox's legal team argues that the planning, zoning, and appeals board lacks the legal jurisdiction to review the plat approval, citing state statutes rendering recorded plats unassailable without landowner consent. Furthermore, the suit alleges that the Village Council violated Florida's Sunshine Law during the abrupt personnel changes. The developer is seeking emergency injunctive relief, a preliminary injunction halting any stop-work orders or retroactive reviews, and declaratory judgments affirming its vested development rights.

A Florida prisoner who claimed he killed his cellmate so he could be moved to death row is set to be executed Tuesday, nearly 18 years after the fatal attack.James Robertson, 63, pleaded guilty to first-degree murder and waived all appeals in the 2008 strangling of Frank Hart. Robertson is set to receive a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke starting at noon.Robertson was supposed to be one of two executions carried out by Florida on Tuesday, but Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant last week for William Lee Thompson. The Republican governor did not provide a reason for withdrawing Thompson’s death warrant but had temporarily stayed his execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation.Records show that this is the first time DeSantis has withdrawn a death warrant, which does not technically change Thompson’s sentence. He will remain on death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future.Robertson's execution comes at a time of escalating attention on the death penalty in the U.S. In Tennessee, Christa Pike survived an execution attempt two weeks ago despite receiving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. And last week, the Pentagon announced that the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan would be livestreamed.According to court records, Robertson was incarcerated at Charlotte Correctional Institution, north of Fort Myers, in December 2008 when he tied several socks together and strangled Hart while the other man slept. Robertson told investigators that the attack was unprovoked and that he killed his cellmate so that he would be sentenced to death, rather than having to live out his days in prison.Robertson was 17 years old when he went to prison in 1980 for burglary and assault. Years of convictions for escape, battery and weapons while in prison kept adding time to his total sentence. Hart was sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction.Robertson pleaded guilty and waived a penalty phase, where a jury would recommend the death penalty or life in prison. A judge sentenced Robertson to death, and he later waived all post-conviction proceedings. Robertson reiterated his position during a hearing earlier this month, telling a judge that he understood his execution had been scheduled and that he didn't want to make any final appeals to the Florida Supreme Court or U.S. Supreme Court.While proponents of the death penalty have long claimed that it is a deterrent, Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty released a statement saying that this case demonstrates the opposite."Frank Hart deserved to be safe in state custody, and his loved ones deserve our compassion," the group's legal and policy director, Maria DeLiberato, said in the statement. "When someone commits murder to try to secure his own execution, we have to confront the conditions that contributed to that decision and the reality that the existence of the death penalty may have caused the very violence it purportedly prevents."Meanwhile, DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson. Bob Graham and Bob Martinez both scheduled executions for Thompson in the 1980s, but years of appeals and stays allowed him to avoid the electric chair, the state's method of execution at the time. The 74-year-old death row inmate was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester.Thompson will remain on Florida’s death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future. His attorneys have said he suffers from dementia, and his health is failing. They said he should be relocated to an adequate medical facility to get the care he needs.Only one other Florida inmate remains alive following a death warrant signed by DeSantis. James Dailey, 80, was scheduled to die in late 2019 for the murder of a 14-year-old girl, but a federal judge halted the execution as attorneys argued against his guilt. The stay was eventually lifted, but DeSantis didn't sign a new death warrant. The state halted all executions during the COVID-19 pandemic and didn't restart until 2023.DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw 19 executions in 2025, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Robertson would be the state's 17th execution of 2026, with two more already scheduled, not counting Thompson.William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed on Oct. 20, followed by Jesse Guardado, 64, on Nov. Reaves was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy after dropping a gun in front of the law enforcement officer in 1986. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.If Robertson, Reaves and Guardado are all executed as planned, that would match the state's 2025 total, with eight weeks remaining in 2026.DeSantis has made few public comments about the unprecedented number of executions but explained previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out."I felt I owed it to them to make sure this ran very smoothly. If I honestly thought someone was innocent, I would not pull the trigger," the governor said last year.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 30 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

Lucie family is turning unimaginable loss into hope after choosing organ donation following the death of their 14-year-old son, who was struck by a vehicle while walking to school, according to police.Port St. Lucie police said the teen was walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. According to transplant advocates, more than 100,000 people nationwide are currently waiting for an organ transplant, and 15 lives are lost each day while patients remain on waiting lists.The teen's family chose organ donation in the days following his death, a decision supporters say can have a profound impact on recipients and their families."It's a courageous thing for them to do, and I think it's the right thing," said St. Lucie County Tax Collector Chris Craft.Craft has worked with Donate Life Florida through the tax collector's office to encourage organ donor registration and raise awareness about the need for donors.For Tyre Gray, a kidney transplant recipient and the chief administrative and legal officer for South Florida Donor Network, the family's decision carries special meaning."Organ donation is one of the few places where grief and gratitude exist in the same place," Gray told WPTV.Gray said he spent five years waiting for a kidney transplant before receiving the life-saving organ he needed."I know for a fact that I wouldn't be here without a family making that election in their deepest moment of despair," he said.Gray described years of uncertainty while waiting for a match."That's five years of uncertainty, five years of being paralyzed, five years of not being able to grow," he said.Organ donation advocates say the need for donors continues across Florida and the United States.Gray noted that a single donor has the potential to save multiple lives and help many more patients through tissue donation."One donor is to save upwards of nine lives and to be able to heal another 75 lives," Gray said.Behind those numbers are people awaiting a second chance, he said."Let's all be heroes and save lives," Gray added.Advocates say organ donation often allows families to find meaning during some of life's most difficult moments."I would hope that they could see the lasting impact that a selfless act can make on others," Craft said. "If you can help somebody else, it's an amazing thing."For transplant recipients, organ donation can mean more time with family, additional milestones and opportunities.In the midst of tragedy, one Port St. Lucie family's decision could now help save lives and ensure their son's legacy continues through the people he may help.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for projects along the Southern Grove, a developing jobs corridor in the city.One of those plans: the long-awaited Costco retail store.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie City Council approves site plan for Costco"This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time,” Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said.Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the 163,000-square-foot store is just the beginning for a new phase of growth in western Port St. Lucie."This is getting closer to the finish line," Samples said.The Costco will join other companies like Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers, calling the Southern Grove area home.McCurry said since the jobs are now here, new commercial development will follow."They see all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see,” said McCurry. "It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here."City council approved two other major site plans for the area, including a 5.5-acre site making up the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District set to bring restaurants and retail."This area has historically been largely underserved by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities,” McCurry said. "It's kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. Some residents in Boca Raton's Spanish Village neighborhood say new construction is changing their community's character, and they're seeking answers after a decades-old oak tree was cut down at a development site.Neighbors reached out to WPTV Boca Raton reporter Victor Jorges with concerns about the growing number of new homes being built in the area. And all of a sudden they came in last week and cut it down."Karolina Michniewicz, another Boca Raton resident, contacted WPTV expressing frustration with the development taking place in her neighborhood."Our beautiful neighborhood is getting pummeled by a developer called Alpha Premium Development," Michniewicz wrote in an email.She criticized the design of the new homes and said neighbors were particularly upset about the loss of mature trees."We are furious as neighbors, and we don't know how to stop it," she wrote.Getting answers from the developerJorges reached out to Alpha Premium Development to find out why the tree was removed despite neighbors saying they were initially told it would be preserved.Jared Niles, a real estate broker for Alpha Premium Development, responded on behalf of the company, clarifying that he is not the builder and does not directly oversee construction operations.Niles said preserving the tree had been part of the original construction plan."From the outset, every effort was made to preserve the existing tree. Palm Beach Atlantic University wrapped up its three-day Hispanic Heritage Festival on Saturday, celebrating Hispanic art, culture and music during Hispanic Heritage Month in South Florida.The annual festival featured a contemporary art exhibition and a series of musical performances designed to showcase the cultural contributions and artistic traditions of the Hispanic world. Organizers say the event continues to grow as it enters its 17th year.In a region with a large Hispanic population, organizers say the festival provides an opportunity for students and community members to engage with artists and musicians while learning more about the diversity of Hispanic cultures.The festival began Thursday with an art exhibition featuring artists representing more than 10 countries.Visitors viewed a wide range of artistic styles and mediums, including oil paintings, photography and metalwork.Among the featured artists was Franco Sotillo, a visual artist originally from Lima, Peru, who said his work combines mixed media and reflects both his heritage and personal experiences."I'm a visual artist and came from Lima, Peru," Sotillo said. "I moved to this country 12 years ago."Sotillo said his work incorporates materials including oils, paper and other raw elements. He said sharing his art allows him to introduce audiences to Peruvian artistic expression."I'm an immigrant, but also bringing my culture to the states to show people how Peruvian art is expressed," Sotillo said.Festival Director Michael O'Connor said the event continues to evolve each year."We're expanding every year," O'Connor said.O'Connor said this year's festival marked the first time organizers expanded programming beyond art and classical music to also include popular music from Hispanic cultures."What we want to do is we want to celebrate the Hispanic artistic heritage, because here in South Florida, especially, we have a very, very large Hispanic population," O'Connor said.Organizers said they hope attendees leave with a deeper appreciation for Hispanic artistic traditions and the people behind them."We hope they'll be inspired too to see the artworks here at the exhibition and to see how the Hispanic world makes itself known through visual arts," O'Connor said. "Not just the art is Hispanic, but also the artists are Hispanic."The festival concluded Saturday with performances featuring both classical and popular Hispanic music.Organizers say they hope the festival continues for many years to come as it celebrates the art, music and cultural heritage that help shape South Florida's diverse communities.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Tuesday that 25 people have been charged in connection with what authorities describe as a large-scale drug trafficking organization responsible for distributing cocaine, fentanyl and methamphetamine across multiple Florida counties.According to investigators, 19 suspects are already in custody and six remain outstanding following a months-long investigation dubbed Operation Ice Breaker.Officials said the investigation targeted a drug trafficking network operating mainly in Palm Beach, Broward and St. Lucie counties, as well as communities in Miami-Dade and Florida's west coast."These was not a users. These were wholesalers," Uthmeier said during a news conference in Boynton Beach "These were large-scale traffickers pushing massive amounts of drugs through our communities."The investigation began in March 2026 and involved the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Office of Statewide Prosecution.Authorities identified Ariel Fernandez Alonso as the primary target of the investigation. Through undercover work and other investigative efforts, agents established probable cause to charge 25 individuals and obtained 21 search warrants, which were served over the past several days.As a result of the operation, investigators said they seized:Approximately 45.5 kilograms of cocaine84 grams of fentanylAbout 2.5 pounds of methamphetaminePrescription pills14 pounds of marijuanaFive rifles11 handguns, including one reported stolenOfficials said several of the suspects face charges including conspiracy to commit racketeering, drug trafficking and unlawful use of a two-way communications device. Uthmeier said some defendants face mandatory minimum prison sentences of 15 years if convicted.Investigators found evidence that large quantities of cocaine were being shipped into Florida from California, with some loads arriving weekly before being distributed throughout South Florida."When you've got investigators finding 20, 30, 40 kilos coming in every single week of cocaine, this is not just a small quantity hand-off," Uthmeier said. "This is a large-scale coordinated network that's passing through massive amounts of drugs."Major Lawrence Poston of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the arrests demonstrate the impact of coordinated law enforcement efforts."When we all combine our efforts together, we can take dangerous, violent individuals like this off the streets," Poston said.FDLE Special Agent in Charge Michael Stein highlighted the role of Florida's State Assistance for Fentanyl Eradication, or SAFE, program, which provides funding and resources for narcotics investigations.According to Stein, since the program was established in 2023, Florida law enforcement agencies have seized nearly 300 kilograms of fentanyl, more than 400 kilograms of cocaine and more than 200 kilograms of methamphetamine. Authorities have also confiscated more than $6 million in cash and over 1,000 firearms while making more than 3,000 arrests.Representatives from the Health Care District of Palm Beach County said local treatment and recovery programs have helped connect thousands of overdose patients with long-term care and support services.Uthmeier said the investigation remains active and additional charges could be filed as authorities continue to follow leads connected to the trafficking network."Our belief is that we've taken down the hub of the operation here in Florida," Uthmeier said. "We'll continue to follow the breadcrumbs and make additional arrests as needed."

A former surgeon turned Wall Street analyst is taking on his city, its mayor and surveillance technology company Flock Safety in federal court. He has no lawyer and wants the city's license plate cameras gone for good. Steven Greer filed the lawsuit in August against Port St. Lucie, Mayor Shannon Martin and Flock Safety, arguing the technology police use to track criminals also threatens Americans' constitutional rights from privacy to gun ownership. "I was appalled at what I learned," Greer told the CBS12 News I-Team. Greer said he spent much of August researching Flock's technology and preparing the federal lawsuit himself. While he has no formal legal training, he says his years working as a surgeon and later on Wall Street prepared him for the technical research and writing involved in representing himself. Flock's automated license plate readers photograph passing vehicles, recording identifying information along with the time and location. Police can search those records to help identify vehicles connected to crimes, but Greer argues the technology also allows officers to reconstruct someone's movements without obtaining a warrant. His amended complaint alleges Port St. Lucie operated 53 Flock cameras and another 73 Axon license plate readers, for a combined network of 126 devices. See also: Brevard County sheriff’s agent killed in wrong-way crash while responding to shooting Greer argues the collection and sharing of that information violates the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. The CBS12 News I-Team has been reporting on Flock cameras since last year, examining how the technology is used by law enforcement and more recently, allegations of misuse. In Fort Pierce, Officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested after investigators accused him of searching his ex-girlfriend's vehicle 382 times. In another case, a woman was arrested and jailed after investigators mistakenly linked her vehicle to a deadly hit-and-run crash. The charges against her were later dropped. Greer cites both cases in his complaint, but argues the larger problem is the surveillance system itself. During their interview, CBS12 I-Team reporter Katie Bente asked Greer about people who aren't concerned about surveillance because they have nothing to hide. "A lot of people say, you know, 'I'm not doing anything wrong. So what does it really matter?'" Bente asked. "Those are the people who don't deserve freedoms. It's just sheer ignorance. They don't even understand why we have a Fourth Amendment," Greer responded. Law enforcement agencies, however, defend license plate readers as valuable investigative tools, crediting the technology with helping identify suspects, recover stolen vehicles and solve crimes. "I know that police have always argued these Flock cameras really help solve crimes. What would be your response to that?" Bente asked. "That's their number one defense. It's not true," Greer said. His assertion is disputed by law enforcement agencies that have documented cases in which license plate reader information helped investigators. Whether the technology is useful in solving crimes is a separate question from whether particular searches are constitutional. Greer's lawsuit also raises an argument not typically associated with traffic cameras: the right to bear arms. He points to Flock cameras reportedly installed at the entrance to the Ocala Shooting Range, a public gun range in Marion County. Greer argues that recording who visits a shooting range could discourage people from exercising their Second Amendment rights. "When I saw that case where they have Flock cameras in gun ranges, I said, 'Whoa, that's a Second Amendment violation,'" Greer told the I-Team. The key buzzword is chilling. You know, if they scare you away from using your gun rights that's a violation." The complaint also challenges the city's handling of public records requests, alleging officials withheld information about camera locations and system audit logs. It includes claims under Florida's constitutional privacy protections and questions the legality of public spending on the network. Greer has also raised First Amendment concerns following a Sept. Lucie City Council meeting. He told the I-Team that the number of police officers present made him feel intimidated and could discourage residents from speaking out. I'm looking around, I see police officers all over the place," Greer said. Meanwhile, the legal debate over Flock is playing out across the country. In Oklahoma, a federal judge ruled Oct. 1 that a warrantless search of approximately a month of license plate location records violated the Fourth Amendment, suppressing evidence obtained following the search. The ruling concerned the specific circumstances of that case and did not establish that all Flock searches are unconstitutional. Law enforcement agencies have continued to defend the technology, while privacy advocates argue that large networks of searchable cameras allow police to monitor ordinary drivers on a scale that wasn't previously possible. Florida is already seeing changes. The Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for automated license plate readers on state highway rights-of-way, requiring their removal from those locations. Lucie also voted to remove 18 of its 53 Flock cameras. But for Greer, taking down some cameras isn't enough. When Bente pointed out that Port St. Lucie was already removing cameras, Greer argued that voluntary decisions can be reversed by future administrations. "The end result is to get a consent decree, where the city and Flock agrees to pull the cameras forever," he said. His amended lawsuit seeks a declaration that the city's surveillance program violates constitutional protections and an injunction restricting operation of the network or national data sharing without a warrant supported by probable cause. It also seeks disputed public records, statutory damages under federal privacy law and litigation costs. Greer told the I-Team that his primary goal is a binding court order, not a financial payout. "I'm not running for office. I'm not seeking attention," he said. "It's my way of doing something." The lawsuit still faces significant legal hurdles, including potential motions to dismiss. A federal judge has not ruled that Port St. Lucie's camera program violates the Constitution. Greer says he's willing to accept help from an attorney, but for now, he's prepared to continue the fight himself. "You cannot have this technology and not violate the Fourth Amendment. There's no way around it," he said. "You've got to get rid of it.

Lucie Boulevard say more needs to be done to protect pedestrians as construction continues on the busy road. Their concerns come after a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student died from injuries he suffered when he was hit by an SUV while walking to school. Police say the freshman was walking along the edge of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on the morning of Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He was pronounced clinically deceased two days later. His family chose to donate his organs . Much of the roadway remains under construction, and there are no sidewalks along large sections of the corridor. Recent heavy rain also left portions of the shoulder flooded, further limiting space for pedestrians. "He was just going to school," said neighbor Irene Ange. "He was just starting his high school year. He had the right to be safe." Irene Ange, who has lived near the boulevard for more than two decades, says students often walk or bike close to traffic, sometimes before sunrise. The stretch of road is dangerous, Ange said. It’s very dark, and drivers are not following the speed limits. Ange said she saw first responders rushing to the crash site and was heartbroken for the student and his family. See also: Suspect booked into Martin County Jail after undercover drug sting, sheriff says The teen’s mother told CBS12 by phone that her son was a people person who made friends easily. She said the family does not want this to happen to another child. The Florida Department of Transportation is widening the southern portion of Port St. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four and adding sidewalks on both sides of the road. FDOT says the sidewalks will be eight to 10 feet wide. The project is expected to be completed in winter 2028, with an estimated cost of about $25.6 million. CBS 12 saw crews building sidewalks several blocks from where the crash happened. FDOT did not respond to questions about what pedestrian safety measures are in place while construction continues. "No accountability with that response because now there's another death," Ange said. Ange says more needs to be done now to keep children safe on their way to school. "This did not have to happen to this family," Ange said. The family now have to mourn him." The driver initially told officers he believed he had struck a construction barrel and has been cooperating with investigators. It remains unclear whether any charges will be filed.

Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for projects along the Southern Grove, a developing jobs corridor in the city.One of those plans: the long-awaited Costco retail store."This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time,” Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said.Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of St. Lucie County Economic Development Council said the 163,000-square-foot store is just the beginning for a new phase of growth in western Port St. Lucie."This is getting closer to the finish line,” Samples said.The Costco will join other companies like Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers, calling the Southern Grove area home.McCurry said since the jobs are now here, new commercial development will follow."They see all the all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see,” said McCurry. “It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here."City council approved two other major site plans for the area, including a 5.5-acre site making up the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District set to bring restaurants and retail.“This area has historically been largely under-served by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities,” McCurry said. “It's kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there's more to come.”The other plan is space for an acute care rehabilitation hospital, featuring inpatient and outpatient services with 42 beds in a more than 55 thousand square foot building."Growing area needs services, and that's just another component of services that are coming into the area is expanded healthcare access,” McCurry said.McCurry said the plans for retail, healthcare and entertainment is fulfilling the city’s master plan for what Southern Grove was destined to become."The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together. What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen,” McCurry said.Samples said Costco still must close on the land, move on to construction design planning and permitting before any shovels hit the ground.
