Crews are making "steady" progress power restoration, and 24 parks have reopened after Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, Gov. Hundreds of thousands of people lost power in the wake of the storm, and 430,000 customers remained without power Saturday morning. As of Sunday afternoon, more than 200,000 customers had power restored, DeSantis said. FLP is expected to be largely finished with power restoration efforts by Monday. CHELCO, which had about 46,000 customers without power as of the press conference, is targeting to have power restored by Tuesday, DeSantis said. "I know it’s frustrating to lose power and some of you have been without it for a couple of days now... Be assured we’re working around the clock to recover from this devastating hurricane," CHELCO CEO Steve Rhodes said. DeSantis held the press conference Sunday evening from Grayton Beach State Park in Santa Rosa Beach. The state park was closed after a bridge washout, but DeSantis said the park was expected to reopen Sunday night after substantial recovery efforts. WATCH HERE The bridge was "totally washed out" after the storm, and FDOT reported the 50-foot-long and 15-foot-deep washout was cutting off access and could "potentially cause harm to the to the beloved Western Lake here in Grayton Beach," DeSantis said. Recovery efforts at the Walton County park involved crews working overnight and bringing in 600 cubic yards of sand to restore the bridge in less than 18 hours, DeSantis said. DeSantis said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida. That damage came primarily from falling trees, debris and other wind damage, as opposed to storm surge, he said. The state plans to submit a major disaster declaration to the federal government, DeSantis said. "There's a certain damage threshold that has to be reached," he said. "I think clearly, just given the amount of trees that fell down on different things, there's going to be more than enough."The disaster declaration, which must be approved by the president, "provides a wide range of federal assistance programs for individuals and public infrastructure, including funds for both emergency and permanent work," according to FEMA. Isaias made landfall in the panhandle Friday night as a Category 2 hurricane. DeSantis has confirmed there were two storm-related deaths in Escambia County.Some of the hardest-hit counties included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers were without power, Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%, according to the governor.Despite the storm's impacts, state emergency officials said Saturday they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.RELATED LINKS:Who to contact during power outagesLeon County deputies deploy to Santa Rosa Co.Firefighters battle house fire amid Hurricane IsaiasWakulla County escapes major damage

The man accused of crossing state lines and traveling to Indian River County to kill his ex-girlfriend was booked into the Indian River County Jail on Monday. According to Indian River County Jail records, Matthew Waggle, 33, was booked into the Indian River County Jail at around 5:20 a.m. He faces a charge of first-degree murder. CBS12 reported on the August shooting after authorities found the victim's body, identified as Dawn Kriskewic , in a roadway in the southern part of the county. Investigators say Waggle traveled to Vero Beach by bus and Uber before allegedly killing Kriskewic outside her home Sunday morning. See also: FHP: Wrong-way driver caused deadly I-95 crash Sunday near PB Lakes Boulevard Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said surveillance video captured Waggle walking through Kriskewic's neighborhood shortly after an Uber dropped him off. Investigators say Waggle then left the area, taking an Uber back to Orlando before boarding another Greyhound bus. He eventually made his way to West Virginia, where investigators say he hid at a motel. Flowers said at the time that Flock Safety cameras were instrumental in tracking down Waggle. Authorities had later tracked Waggle to a motel in West Virginia and taken him into custody. Authorities said Kriskewic had ended her relationship with Waggle before the shooting and had warned coworkers at the hair salon that she wanted no contact with him.

Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

Lake Worth Beach is reducing fines for bulk and vegetation pickup violations and issuing partial refunds to residents after public backlash over 12-hundred citations issued since August.The city said more than 1,200 violations were issued after enforcement began Aug. 9 under its bulk trash and vegetation pickup rules. Residents complained they were unaware of the stricter enforcement and said they received costly citations without warning.The change comes after concerns raised by residents. Luis Carvajal, a Lake Worth Beach resident since 2009, contacted WPTV after receiving a bill that included a $335 violation charge.Carvajal said landscapers working on his property had trimmed palm fronds and placed them near the street for pickup."They're still continuing to work in the backyard or whatever. And there are trucks out here, and then the city solid waste comes by and they scoop it up and they leave. Okay, I didn't think nothing of it," Carvajal told WPTV's Michael Hoffman.Days later, he received a bill in the mail."Make it make sense to me. It didn't make sense," Carvajal said. "They're Palm Beach prices."Carvajal said he had never previously received a city violation notice.Concerns about the fines quickly spread among residents and eventually reached the Lake Worth Beach City Commission.According to city officials, though the changes went into effect in October 2025, more than 1,200 violations were issued after enforcement began in August, generating widespread criticism from residents who said they were not adequately informed about the rules.Vice Mayor Mimi May acknowledged residents frustrations during recent commission discussions."As somebody who's sitting here all the time, I'm like, how do you not know that?" May said. "But if I was just a non-informed resident, I would be upset about that."May is one of the officials who helped spearhead the changes when the ordinance took effect in October 2025.At the time, she recommended fines as high as $500 and opposed sending notification letters to residents before enforcement began.Now, she has changed her position."$300 is way too much money for people on a fixed income," May said.The vice mayor also issued a public apology on social media."I sincerely apologize for any confusion or frustration this situation has caused. I understand that a $335 fine can be a significant financial burden, especially when someone may not have fully understood the rules," May wrote.City leaders have now approved changes to the penalty structure.The city has reduced the violation fine from $335 to $135. Officials also plan to reimburse affected residents $200 for each violation issued under the previous rate.For residents like Carvajal, the city's decision comes as welcome news."That's great news, and I thank Channel 5 for looking into this matter," he told WPTV's Michael Hoffman.City officials say the reduced fines are now in effect, and eligible residents will receive reimbursements related to previous violations on their next bill.

Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms was found guilty of a third-degree felony of official misconduct and not guilty of a second-degree felony of bid tampering on Thursday.Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct.WATCH BELOW: Former Fort Pierce city manager found guilty of official misconductAccording to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms was accused of rigging the bidding process for two vacant parcels of land along Avenue D, adjacent to the Lincoln Theater, in favor of a local nonprofit, Lincoln Park Young Professionals.Among that nonprofit's board was Caleta Scott, Mimms' niece, and also a city employee.The nonprofit had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegheny Franciscan Ministries for a community center project, but nothing was ever built.Johnathan Bridges, special assistant state attorney and Brandon White, major crimes attorney for the 19th Circuit, said there was a mountain of evidence, including emails and city documents that incriminated Mimms."What we learned is millions of dollars have been wasted by this city hall under the leadership of Nick Mimms, and for too long, it went unchecked,” said White. Pierce deserve better, and I think this verdict shows the corruption that was happening under Nick Mimms. It's about time someone was held accountable."WPTV pressed Mimms and his attorney for comment as they left the courtroom but did not get a response.Mimms was granted a pre-sentencing investigation and is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. Lucie County Courthouse.Prosecutors said he could face a maximum of five years in prison.

Florida Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov received the Key to the City of Boca Raton at a ceremony Thursday afternoon.It was awarded to Barkov by Mayor Andy Thomson. Barkov has lived in Boca Raton since he was 18, his first year with the Panthers.Watch report from Mike TrimWPTV Florida Panthers Anchor and Panthers 360 host Mike Trim connected with Barkov at the ceremony.Trim asked, why is Boca Raton so special to you? Barkov said “Because I live there, I live there in my whole career which is almost half of my lifetime so, I only live into two places. It’s back home in Finland and focus so this is a special place for me.” Trim then asked, “Are there any Barky favorites in Boca Raton, places that you really like to go?”Barkov said, “There's a lot. I play a lot of tennis, so every park has a tennis court. I love a lot of different restaurants. Mizner Park is super nice. There's so many good things about it. I will be here all day explaining.”Panthers television play-by-play announcer Steve Goldstein emceed today’s event. Many fans also met Barkov. The Panthers all-time franchise points leader, Barkov, is currently out 6-8 weeks rehabbing a leg injury but tells Trim he is excited to get back on the ice. Trim asked, “A lot of fans in Palm Beach county are wondering how your doing after what happened on the road trip. Is there anything you want to say about that?"Barkov said, “I mean, I got really good news after the road trip, so really looking forward to trying to come back as soon as possible. We have good doctors, they take really good care of me, so I'm really lucky about that.”

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Polls Residents on Paying $11 More a Month for Extra Trash Pickup
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie is asking residents in a nonbinding straw poll whether they would support paying roughly $11 more per month, about $131 more a year, for a second weekly trash pickup. Residents currently get one garbage pickup per week, and the additional service could start in 2028 if the City Council decides to move forward.

Scott Samples, spokesperson for the city of Port St. Lucie, said the poll is meant to gauge public opinion rather than set policy. "This is something that is nonbinding, but it gives City Council an opportunity to get a sense of the will of the people and what they would prefer to see," Samples said. A "yes" vote would show support for the added cost, while a "no" vote would signal opposition, but the results will not automatically change the current pickup schedule.

Any change to trash service still has to go through the City Council, which controls the city's solid-waste contract and service levels. That means council members would need to approve any new schedule and reach an updated agreement with the city's current waste provider, FCC Environmental Services. The city also noted that adding a second weekly pickup would become an ongoing expense that could rise over time with inflation.

"City Council would take this up. They would have to work with the vendor to understand what the logistics of that would be. And then, the City Council would then vote on whether or not to move forward with this," Samples said. City officials say the poll is designed to give council members insight into what residents want before any formal proposal comes up for a vote, but the final call on whether Port St. Lucie households pay more for twice-weekly trash pickup rests with the council.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound Shooting Victim Dies; No Arrest as Martin County Weighs Stand Your Ground
hero.body:
The man shot by his best friend in Hobe Sound earlier this week has died, and no arrest has been made as the Martin County Sheriff's Office works with the State Attorney's Office to determine whether the shooting was self-defense. Jarvis Preston, 21, of Hobe Sound, died Thursday, according to the Sheriff's Office. His mother, Ebony Preston, identified him and said he was not married and was the father of a small child.

The Sheriff's Office began investigating after the shooting Wednesday night on Southeast Citrus Way, off Florida Avenue, in the Banner Lake neighborhood. Neighbors reported hearing three gunshots around 8 p.m. Sheriff John Budensiek said Preston and his friend had been drinking earlier in the day and that Preston tried to rob his friend near their homes. "Multiple witnesses have now told us that he made threats to all kinds of people out on the street. He was yelling loudly, was extremely intoxicated, acting belligerent," Budensiek said.

According to Budensiek, the friend, who was armed with an AR15 assault rifle, came out of his house twice with his girlfriend. During the second encounter, the friend and Preston, who was armed with a handgun fitted with a 30-round magazine, got into a confrontation that ended in gunfire. "The deceased (Preston) starts to pull out a handgun. Actually, it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest and he (Preston) drops right there," Budensiek said. The handgun was recovered at the scene. Preston was taken to St. Mary's Medical Center in West Palm Beach, where he died.

Budensiek said the shooter attempted to render aid to Preston and remained at the scene afterward. Preston's mother and stepfather, Rodney Clemon, said they are struggling to understand how the confrontation escalated between two close friends. "It's dreadful, like, I can't, I can't understand what, why it expired to the way it did, because they, best friends. What escalated this to happen when it did?" Ebony Preston said. "It's lot of unanswered questions. But my son is dead, so how do we go from there?"

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Residents Push Back on $6.1 Million Prima Vista Boulevard Plan
hero.body:
St. Lucie County held its first public workshop on a proposed $6.1 million redesign of Prima Vista Boulevard Thursday at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center, and most residents who attended said they doubted it would make the road safer. The plan would replace the center turn lane on the stretch between Aroso Boulevard and U.S. 1 with a raised median and add landscaping meant to make the road feel narrower and encourage drivers to slow down.

County officials said the goal is to improve safety, reduce crashes, and slow traffic along the corridor. St. Lucie County engineer Dan Zrallack acknowledged the resistance from residents during the meeting. "We understand it's not popular. That's why we have these," Zrallack said. "We're taking away the ease of access for people who live along this corridor. There's a lot of driveways. There's a lot of residences that have historically been able to turn directly into their driveway. It's no longer safe to do that. We have to control the traffic so that we have less accidents."

Many of the community members who spoke at the workshop said they were not convinced the changes would actually reduce crashes or improve conditions on the corridor. County staff estimate the project would cost about $6.

County leaders said the feedback gathered at Thursday's session will help shape the project going forward. The proposal remains in its early stages, and the county still needs to design the roadway and secure funding before any construction can begin. Residents who missed the workshop can review the plans and submit comments to Christopher.arnold@stlucieco.gov.

Jarvis Preston, 21, of Hobe Sound has died from injuries suffered in a shooting Wednesday night on Southeast Citrus Way in the Banner Lake neighborhood, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. No arrest has been made, and Sheriff John Budensiek says investigators have not yet determined whether the shooting was self-defense or a crime.

Neighbors reported hearing three gunshots around 8 p.m. Wednesday. Sheriff Budensiek said Preston and his friend had been drinking earlier in the day and that Preston tried to rob the friend near their homes. The friend, armed with an AR15 assault rifle, came out of his house twice with his girlfriend before the two men confronted each other. "The deceased (Preston) starts to pull out a handgun. cards.headline: Rescued Hobe Sound Kittens Buried Alive Recovering in Foster Care
cards.teaser: Kali and Amara, the two kittens pulled alive from a backyard burial site in Hobe Sound, are gaining strength with a foster family and could be ready for adoption within weeks.
cards.body:
Two kittens rescued last week after being buried alive in Hobe Sound are recovering steadily in foster care and could be ready for adoption in four to six weeks, according to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies pulled the kittens, now named Kali and Amara, from the ground after 36-year-old Alba Chavez allegedly buried multiple kittens alive because she believed they were demons. Two other kittens were found dead at the scene, and a fifth remains missing. Chavez faces criminal charges in the case and is being held on an Immigration and Customs Enforcement hold, according to the sheriff's office.

Body camera video released by the Martin County Sheriff's Office shows deputies digging to reach the kittens, with one deputy expressing surprise that the animals were still alive during the rescue. The roughly 4-week-old kittens were initially lethargic after being pulled from the ground but have since become increasingly active.

When the Humane Society needed a foster home for the survivors, local nurse Jennifer Jagdeo and her family stepped in right away. "As an animal lover, I think we're all shocked by it," Jagdeo said. "For me, my focus has been them and healing them." She said the kittens have made steady progress under around-the-clock care. "They're walking around now, they wrestle with each other and play," Jagdeo said. "They drink the bottle like it's nobody's business. They're just little joys." Her son, Ryland Vick, said he was saddened by what happened to the kittens. "Why would they do this when they're just so cute?" he said.

Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said the organization continues to respond to difficult animal welfare cases across the region, including large-scale rescue and hoarding investigations. "We hope that there's an end to it, and it just doesn't seem like there's an end to it," Fisher said. "But we're always here for the animals. We're always ready." The Humane Society is seeking additional foster families willing to temporarily care for animals awaiting permanent homes, and the organization is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund, which helps cover veterinary care for animals rescued from cruelty and neglect. Jagdeo said she hopes Kali and Amara eventually find permanent homes together. "My hope is that they find somebody that needs them as much as they need their human," she said.

cards._canonical_context_headline: Sheriff: Deputies Heard Kittens Crying Underground in Hobe Sound Burial Case
cards._canonical_context_body:
Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek on Friday gave new details on the arrest of a Hobe Sound woman accused of killing two kittens and burying two others alive, revealing that deputies heard the animals crying from beneath the ground during a backyard search. Alba Chavez, 36, faces four felony counts of animal torture after deputies said she buried kittens up to 3 feet underground at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park, with two kittens rescued alive and two found dead. A fifth kitten remains missing despite repeated searches of the property.

Deputies responded to the mobile home park Thursday night after several minors inside the home called 911 to report that Chavez had killed two kittens on Monday, placed them in the trash and later buried them in the backyard. The children, fearing for three remaining kittens, had locked them inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday night. When they returned, they found the bedroom door forced open and the kittens gone, prompting the call to law enforcement. Deputies found Chavez standing in the roadway, and she reportedly admitted to killing the two kittens, telling deputies she believed the animals had demons, calling them ugly and saying she did not want black or brown cats in the home.

Chavez then led deputies to the backyard where the kittens had been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. As deputies dug through the rain-soaked ground, they heard cries coming from underground. Two kittens were pulled out alive and rushed to an emergency veterinary facility, where they were being treated for dehydration. The sheriff said veterinarians were also concerned about possible injuries from lack of oxygen while the animals were buried, and he said the kittens could still die from their injuries despite being rescued. The two kittens killed Monday were found dead at the burial site.

cards.headline: Stuart's Atlantic Diving Team trains young divers toward scholarships and Olympic goals
cards.teaser: Young divers with Stuart's Atlantic Diving Team are training under coach Pito Alberty with hopes of college scholarships, international competition and the Olympics.
cards.body:
A group of young divers in Stuart is training with hopes that their sport will carry them to college scholarships, international competition and even the Olympics. The athletes train with the Atlantic Diving Team under coach Osvaldo "Pito" Alberty, who teaches divers of all ages, backgrounds and experience levels the Olympic sport of diving.

Grace Erickson, a local diver now in eighth grade, said diving has been her passion since early childhood. "On my preschool poster I wrote what I wanted to be when I got older was a diver," Erickson said. She said the sport keeps surprising her. "It's been really exciting; it's new things every twist and turn, both in your head and diving off the board," Erickson said. Erickson said she has come to love platform diving in particular, along with the friendships she has built with teammates over the years. She hopes to take her diving to the college level.

Alberty, who has coached Erickson for years, said he wants to see her and her teammates push the sport to new heights. "We are like a family here. We treat each other with respect and courtesy, and we push each other to do better than everyone else," Alberty said. He said starting divers young opens doors down the road. "The younger we get them, the better it is because over time they can get scholarships. If they want to do international diving, they can qualify for international competitions or even the Olympics," Alberty said.

Among the team's newer members is 14-year-old Carissa Smith, who switched from gymnastics to diving about two months ago. Smith said her gymnastics background has helped her adjust to the new sport, though she has not yet competed because she wants to master the basics first. "I was recently a gymnast and just about two months ago I started diving," Smith said. She said the sport has already won her over. "It feels like you're flying; it's exhilarating just being able to get better at my diving," Smith said.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Residents Push Back on Prima Vista Boulevard Safety Plan
hero.body:
Most residents who attended a St. Lucie County information session Thursday on proposed safety changes to Prima Vista Boulevard said they oppose the plan, arguing it would not make the road safer. The session, held at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center, focused on a proposal to redesign the stretch of Prima Vista Boulevard between Aroso Boulevard and U.S. 1. The plan would replace the center turn lane with a raised median and add landscaping intended to make the road feel narrower and encourage drivers to slow down.

County officials said the changes are meant to improve safety, reduce crashes, and slow traffic along the corridor. During the meeting, however, a majority of the community members who spoke said they did not believe the proposed redesign would achieve that goal. County leaders said the feedback collected at the session will help shape how the project moves forward.

The proposal remains in its early stages. St. Lucie County still needs to design the roadway, estimate project costs, and identify funding sources before any construction work can begin. No funding has been secured for the project at this point.

Residents who were unable to attend Thursday's workshop can still review the plans and submit comments by emailing Christopher.arnold@stlucieco.gov.

hero.headline: Flock Cameras Help Indian River Deputies Catch Suspect in Grandfather's Death
hero.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested a 35-year-old man early Thursday after a cross-county chase ended in a Walmart parking lot, following the discovery of his grandfather's body in Okeechobee County. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief announced the arrest of Earl Douglas Wadlington III during a Thursday press conference, tying it to the homicide of 88-year-old veteran Paul Eugene Baker.

The case began when Baker's daughter-in-law requested a welfare check after not hearing from him for several days. She went to his residence and found the house in disarray, which investigators called highly unusual. "She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazellief said. Law enforcement obtained and executed a search warrant for the property and found Baker dead. Investigators said the manner and location of his death made it immediately evident that it was a homicide. Baker's vehicle and other property were also missing. Investigators learned Wadlington had recently been living with his grandfather after no other family member would take him in. Hazellief said Wadlington has more than 800 felonies in his criminal background. "The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazellief said.

Because the daughter-in-law held power of attorney for Baker, deputies entered the missing vehicle into the ALPR license plate reader system shared with partner agencies across the Treasure Coast, flagging it as connected to a homicide suspect. Investigators tracked the vehicle leaving the area but withheld a public alert. "We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazellief said. The agency was required this past month to remove Flock cameras from state roads and certain permitted locations under a Florida Department of Transportation order, but cameras at other qualifying locations remained active. "To be specific with the language, we still have them in place in places that don't meet that criteria, and because of that, we were able to really move forward with this case," Hazellief said. Senior detective Ashley Rojas led the investigation, according to Hazellief.

Indian River County's Flock camera system detected the stolen vehicle Thursday morning, leading deputies to Wadlington's location. Flowers described the roughly 4 a.m. pursuit, which was captured on video, as Wadlington fled through a Walmart parking lot. "One of the particular things that's interesting is it's 4 o'clock in the morning. He's running from our deputies. He's running through the Walmart parking lot. You see that our deputies were able to deploy stop sticks. The reason that he ultimately stopped and got out and ran is because his truck was going to stop working. That stolen vehicle is going to stop working," Flowers said. The Sebastian Police Department assisted Indian River County deputies throughout the chase. "Doesn't matter if the uniform is green or blue, doesn't matter what color it is. We're all going to go after the bad guys," Flowers said.

Flowers defended the county's continued use of Flock cameras despite public criticism of the system. "For all the naysayers and all the people who don't like flock and who don't like it, we're going to continue to use it. We're going to continue to put bad guys in jail because of it," Flowers said. He noted the cameras not covered by the state DOT order remain in operation and have aided other cases, including one involving a missing elderly woman. Wadlington was arrested on charges of fleeing and eluding, and driving a stolen vehicle. Both agencies said they are working closely with the state attorney's office to obtain a warrant charging him with homicide. "This guy is the definition of somebody who needs to stay behind bars," Flowers said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Proposes Raised Median for Prima Vista Boulevard After 578 Crashes
hero.body:
St. Lucie County is proposing to remove the center left-turn lanes on Prima Vista Boulevard between Airoso Boulevard and U.S. Highway 1 and replace them with a raised median. County staff are presenting the designs and seeking input from neighbors on the project.

County engineer Dan Zrallack said the center turn lane is often called a "suicide lane" because more turning movements create more chances for accidents. He said the raised median will let the county control where turning movements happen, protecting both drivers and pedestrians along the roadway.

According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, that stretch of Prima Vista Boulevard has had 578 crashes since 2020. Zrallack said the median is intended to make the road safer.

hero.headline: Witnesses: Hobe Sound Man Was Armed, Drunk Before Friend Shot Him
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek is reviewing whether Florida's Stand Your Ground law applies in the fatal shooting of 21-year-old Jarvis Preston, who was killed Wednesday night by a lifelong friend during a confrontation in the Banner Lake neighborhood of Hobe Sound. New details released by the sheriff show witnesses said Preston had been drinking heavily throughout the day and began threatening the shooter and others while armed with a handgun before he was shot.

Martin County sheriff's deputies responding to Southeast Citrus Way found Preston with three gunshot wounds to the chest. Budensiek said Preston and the shooter were friends and described how the confrontation escalated. "He's talking, I'm going to shoot you, I'm going to hurt you. The shooter walks towards him, now they're at the edge of the road, at which point the deceased starts to pull out a handgun. The shooter pulls out his AR-15, actually it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest, and he drops right there," Budensiek said.

The sheriff said the shooter called 911 and attempted life-saving efforts on Preston before he was flown to St. Mary's Hospital, where he died. Budensiek said investigators have not yet determined whether the shooting will be classified as self-defense. "I know you're going to ask me, was it a stand your ground? And the answer is, I don't know right now," Budensiek said. No arrest has been made as the sheriff's office continues to evaluate the circumstances of the shooting.

Preston's grandmother, Harriet Ford Gregg, said she heard the gunshots and went outside to find her grandson on the ground. "It was Jarvis laying on the ground out there, and the police officer was reviving him," Gregg said. Preston lived with his grandmother, and she said she has been unable to bring herself to enter his bedroom since his death. "I'm not going in there," Gregg said.

cards.headline: Banner Lake Neighbors Mourn as Deputies Weigh Charges in Fatal Shooting
cards.teaser: Investigators are reviewing surveillance footage and witness accounts to determine whether a Hobe Sound man's fatal shooting of his lifelong friend qualifies as self-defense under Florida's Stand Your Ground law.
cards.body:
A 21-year-old Hobe Sound man died after being shot by a man the Martin County Sheriff's Office describes as his friend, and neighbors in the tight-knit Banner Lake community are now grieving the loss while investigators determine whether the shooting qualifies as self-defense under Florida's Stand Your Ground law. The shooting happened on SE Citrus Way in Banner Lake, and the victim has been identified as Jarvis Preston. The Martin County Sheriff is still weighing whether the facts support a homicide charge or a Stand Your Ground defense, and the man who fired the shots has been detained for questioning but has not been publicly identified.

According to the sheriff's office, Preston and the man had been drinking together Wednesday afternoon. Detectives believe Preston kept drinking into the evening, then tried to rob his friend. The friend got away, but investigators say Preston followed him home and threatened him there. "The deceased starts to pull out a handgun. Shooter pulls his AR-15, acts a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest, and he drops right there," said John Budensiek of the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Investigators say that after the shooting, the shooter dropped his weapon, took the handgun away from Preston, and began rendering aid until deputies arrived.

Detectives are now searching for surveillance video and interviewing witnesses as they work to determine whether Stand Your Ground applies. "We're really not ready to make that determination. But I want to make sure we do it the right way to send the right messages to the right people, so this doesn't happen again," Budensiek said.

The shooting has shaken Banner Lake, where neighbor Stephanie Rose said she knew both men. "It's just sad, really sad," Rose said. "They were good kids, I mean they got a long perfect, I mean they were friends. I don't know what happened." As Preston's family and neighbors come to terms with his death, Rose said she had been planning to pay her respects in person. "Unbelievable and it's just sad. I was just on my way to give them my condolences," she said.

The vote gives county administration the green light to begin negotiations with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county’s public bus system. For former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence, Tuesday’s decision offered a sign of hope after he and several other drivers suddenly lost their jobs last Thursday. “I’m hoping that we get this back on the road soon. During Tuesday’s county commission meeting, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton explained that county officials had spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. “We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us,” Gorton said. According to Gorton, the county evaluated several proposals before identifying MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county’s emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million. During that year, county officials would work toward establishing a standard multi-year contract through the county’s normal competitive bidding process. One of the county’s priorities during negotiations is bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs following last week’s shutdown. “We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible,” Gorton said. hero.headline: Grandson Arrested After Chase in Vero Beach in Okeechobee Veteran's Death
hero.body:
A welfare check on an 88-year-old Okeechobee County veteran led investigators to a homicide and ended with the arrest of the victim's grandson following a pre-dawn police chase through Vero Beach, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers and Okeechobee County Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief said Thursday. Paul Eugene Baker, a longtime Okeechobee County resident, was found dead on his property. His grandson, 35-year-old Earl Douglas Wadlington III, was taken into custody around 4 a.m. after deputies pursued him through a Walmart parking lot and deployed stop sticks to disable the stolen truck he was driving. Hazellief called it "a tragedy and a family tragedy" that began as a simple welfare check.

The case started when Baker's daughter-in-law, who had not heard from him in several days, went to check on his residence and found the house in disarray. "She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazellief said. Deputies obtained and executed a search warrant, finding Baker dead on the property in a manner investigators said made clear right away that it was a homicide. His only vehicle and other property were missing from the home. Investigators learned Wadlington had recently been living with Baker after no other relative would take him in, given his lengthy criminal history of more than 800 felonies. "The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazellief said.

Because the daughter-in-law held power of attorney for Baker, investigators were able to enter his missing vehicle into the ALPR license plate reader network shared among Treasure Coast agencies, flagging it as connected to a homicide suspect. Deputies tracked the vehicle but withheld a public alert to avoid tipping off the driver. "We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazellief said. Though the agency recently had to remove Flock cameras from state roads under a Department of Transportation order, cameras at other qualifying locations remained active, which Hazellief said was key to advancing the case. Senior detective Ashley Rojas led the investigation.

Indian River County's Flock system detected the stolen vehicle, leading deputies to Wadlington early Thursday. Flowers said the truck was rigged to stop running, which is why Wadlington eventually got out and fled on foot through the Walmart lot before being caught. Sebastian Police assisted during the chase. Wadlington faces charges of fleeing and eluding and driving a stolen vehicle, and both agencies said they are working with the state attorney's office to secure a warrant charging him with homicide. hero.headline: After Fatal Crash, Neighbors Press FDOT for Lighting on Port St. Lucie Boulevard
hero.body:
Neighbors along Port St. Lucie Boulevard are calling for better lighting after a fatal crash last week, saying the ongoing road-widening project has left the corridor dangerous for pedestrians and drivers, especially at night. The Florida Department of Transportation has not said whether it will add any interim safety measures in response.

Howard Shapiro, who lives near the construction zone, said the roadway has no lighting outside at night, which worries him because children walk along it to reach nearby schools. "I don't walk around here... no lighting outside at nighttime. Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there," Shapiro said. He said a new sidewalk being installed as part of the project will help, but added that street lights need to follow.

FDOT is overseeing construction along a stretch of Port St. Lucie Boulevard between Alcantara Boulevard and Parr Drive. The project began in 2025 and involves widening the road from two lanes to four, along with adding new sidewalks and lighting, according to FDOT's website.

Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said the completed project will improve both safety and traffic flow on the roadway. "We'll see a significant improvement in the safety as well as the traffic flow for this roadway," Samples said. When asked whether city staff could provide any temporary safety measures while construction continues, Samples said the work falls under FDOT's responsibility. "It's tough when there is active, ongoing construction, because people still need to utilize it," Samples said. "That's why we encourage everyone to do it as safely as they possibly can.

hero.headline: AmeriCorps Literacy Mentors Return to Martin County Boys & Girls Clubs
hero.teaser: After a funding-driven hiatus, AmeriCorps volunteers are back at four Martin County Boys & Girls Clubs with a goal of reaching 575 K-5 students and boosting literacy skills by 65%.
hero.body:
AmeriCorps literacy mentors are returning to the Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County after a funding-driven pause, with new goals for reaching young readers across the county. The federal mentorship program places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support, and organizers aim to serve 575 kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys & Girls Club locations.

The Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County first brought AmeriCorps to the area in 2019. For six years, volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause. Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said the program's absence was keenly felt. "We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward," Maine said.

AmeriCorps Program Director for the Martin County Boys & Girls Club, Russell Lamberti, said the program has set a specific target for its return. "We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar," Lamberti said. AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar said the mission carries personal meaning for him as well. "I am a Haitian American. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow," Cesar said.

The Boys & Girls Clubs says the program delivered strong results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4, and about the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization. Students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns. Beyond the classroom, AmeriCorps members completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service.

The program's return comes as literacy remains a countywide priority. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments. The AmeriCorps initiative is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs and offers after-school academic assistance through certified teachers. The organization also runs programs including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs.

cards.headline: Martin County Moves to Restore MARTY Bus Service With $3M Contract
cards.teaser: County commissioners unanimously authorized emergency talks with MTM Transit to bring back MARTY bus service, with hopes buses could run again next week.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator negotiate a new one-year contract worth approximately $3 million with MTM Transit, a company that previously ran the county's public bus system. The vote comes days after MARTY public bus service abruptly shut down last Thursday, leaving riders without service and drivers without jobs.

Martin County Transit LLC, the company that had been operating MARTY, stopped service suddenly, citing rising operating costs including fuel and maintenance. Bill Lawrence, a former MARTY bus driver who lost his job in the shutdown, said Tuesday's vote gave him hope. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials spent the days following the shutdown searching for a way to restore service. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. After reviewing several proposals, the county identified MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county's emergency procurement rules, the new agreement would run for one year while officials work toward a standard multi-year contract through the county's normal competitive bidding process.

Gorton said bringing back the drivers laid off last week is a priority in the negotiations. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating the county's previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials said they hope to finalize negotiations with MTM Transit by the end of this week, which could allow buses to resume running as soon as next week.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Voters to Decide Sales Tax Renewal, Mosquito Control Expansion
cards.teaser: November's ballot asks St. Lucie County voters to renew a half-cent infrastructure sales tax for another decade and to expand mosquito control service into Tradition and the southwest county.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County voters will decide two ballot questions in November tied to the county's growing population and its strain on infrastructure and services. The first question asks voters to renew the existing half-cent sales tax, originally approved in 2018 and set to expire in two years, for another decade. The measure is not a new tax and would keep the total sales tax rate at 7%, with the half-cent portion continuing to fund infrastructure projects such as road improvements, sidewalks and stormwater drainage, along with larger projects like widening St. Lucie County roadways.

"Now we're seeing that impact, you know, the delayed maintenance and the increased growth we've seen picked up, we're starting to have to play catch-up with those infrastructure projects and the needs are still there," said Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County.

The second ballot question asks voters whether to expand the county's mosquito control district to include the Tradition area and southwestern St. Lucie County, regions that have grown beyond the district's current service boundaries. Mosquito control services currently cover about half of the county's 600 square miles. If voters approve the expansion, affected property owners in those areas would pay about $28 more per year in taxes to fund fogging, spraying and mosquito surveillance.

hero.headline: Matt Gaetz, Joel Greenberg Named in New Federal Sex Trafficking Lawsuit
hero.body:
Former Florida Republican U.S. Congressman Matt Gaetz is among the defendants named in a new federal civil lawsuit filed on behalf of two women identified as Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2. The complaint also names former Seminole County Tax Collector Joel Greenberg and several other defendants.

The lawsuit alleges that from 2017 through January 2019, Gaetz and Greenberg "coordinated recruitment, payments, drugs, and travel to obtain commercial sexual acts." West Palm Beach attorney Spencer Kuvin, who represents the plaintiffs, said the complaint was written in detail by design.

"We wanted the courts to understand the full breadth of this operation," Kuvin said. He said attorneys for the plaintiffs believe communications referenced in the complaint, particularly text messages, support the allegations. "The text messages we have we believe are incredibly damaging to Mr. Greenberg," Kuvin said.

Gaetz left Congress in 2024 and has previously denied wrongdoing connected to allegations investigated by the House Ethics Committee. Greenberg, the former Seminole County tax collector, is currently serving federal prison time following his conviction in a separate criminal case. The allegations in the civil complaint are claims made by the plaintiffs and have not been proven in court.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound Shooting Victim Dies, No Arrest Made in Banner Lake Case
hero.body:
A person shot during a Wednesday night shooting in Hobe Sound has died, the Martin County Sheriff's Office confirmed Thursday, marking a grim turn in a case that still has no arrest despite two people being questioned by investigators. The shooting occurred in the Banner Lake neighborhood, and deputies have not released information identifying a suspect or a motive as the investigation continues.

The sheriff's office opened its investigation Wednesday night after the shooting took place on Southeast Citrus Way, just off Florida Avenue. Residents in the area reported hearing three gunshots at around 8 p.m. The victim was airlifted to St. Mary's Hospital with injuries described by deputies as life-threatening at the time.

During the course of the investigation, one person was detained and a second individual was questioned by authorities. However, as of Thursday morning, neither person remained in custody and no charges had been filed. The sheriff's office later confirmed that the victim succumbed to injuries sustained in the shooting, elevating the case from a non-fatal shooting to a death investigation.

The case remains active, and no further details about a possible suspect, motive, or the relationship between the victim and those questioned have been made public. The shooting is one of several violent incidents reported recently across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County region, though it stands on its own as an open case with the Martin County Sheriff's Office continuing to work to determine what led to the gunfire on Southeast Citrus Way.

cards.headline: Martin County Commissioners Vote to Negotiate $3M Deal to Restore MARTY Bus Service
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners voted unanimously to negotiate a one-year, $3 million contract with MTM Transit after MARTY bus service abruptly shut down last week, with officials hoping to rehire displaced drivers.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator begin negotiating a new contract with MTM Transit to restore MARTY public bus service, which abruptly shut down last Thursday. The proposed deal, allowed under the county's emergency procurement rules, would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million.

MARTY service stopped last week when Martin County Transit LLC, the company that had been operating the system, cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as reasons for discontinuing service. The shutdown left several drivers suddenly out of work, including Bill Lawrence, who said Tuesday's vote gave him hope. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials spent the past several days exploring options to bring service back. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county evaluated several proposals before settling on MTM Transit, a company that has previously operated the county's bus system, as its preferred choice. During the one-year contract period, county officials plan to work toward a standard multi-year agreement through the county's normal competitive bidding process.

Gorton said bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs is a top priority in the negotiations. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating the county's previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials said they hope to finalize negotiations with MTM Transit by the end of this week, which could allow buses to resume operating as early as next week.

hero.headline: Former Officer Otto Lenke Sentenced to Death for Fort Pierce Bike Shop Murder
hero.body:
A judge has sentenced Otto Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, to death for the 2021 murder of Richard Benson, a Fort Pierce bike shop owner. Benson's family watched the sentencing via Zoom from out of state and was not present in the courtroom.

Assistant State Attorney Brandon White, who prosecuted the case, said jealousy drove the killing. Benson had started dating a woman Lenke previously dated. During the sentencing hearing, prosecutors showed jurors security video from inside the bike shop that they said captured Lenke not just killing Benson but torturing him beforehand. "He tormented him and basically made Richard's life a living hell, those last two minutes of his life by pouring that accelerant on him and lighting him on fire," White said.

White said Lenke used more than 20 years of law enforcement experience to plan and carry out the attack, believing his background would help him escape detection. "The defendant used his 20-plus years of experience in law enforcement to plan this attack, to carry out this attack," White said. He called the crime one of the most heinous in the circuit's history, noting it was captured on camera and carefully planned. "The jury got it right," White said. "This was probably one of the most heinous crimes in the history of our circuit. It was all caught on camera. It was well planned out."

The case is not finished. Florida law requires the state Supreme Court to review all death sentences, and Lenke is expected to appeal his conviction. White said he believes the sentence delivers the outcome Benson's family sought. "I think this is something they wanted for Rich. This was justice," White said.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Neighbors Push for Lighting on Boulevard After Fatal Crash
cards.teaser: Residents along Port St. Lucie Boulevard say the under-construction corridor needs street lights now, after a fatal crash left them worried about pedestrians and drivers in the dark.
cards.body:
Residents along Port St. Lucie Boulevard are calling for street lighting and other interim safety measures following a fatal crash on the roadway, which is in the middle of a Florida Department of Transportation widening project. Neighbor Howard Shapiro said the road lacks lighting, particularly in the early morning and at night, posing a risk to the children who walk along it to nearby schools.

"I don't walk around here... no lighting outside at nighttime. Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there," Shapiro said. He said the sidewalk FDOT is installing as part of the project will help, but that street lights need to be added as well. "They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's gonna be helpful. But street lights need to follow," he said.

FDOT is overseeing construction on a segment of Port St. Lucie Boulevard between Alcantara Boulevard and Parr Drive. The agency began work on the project in 2025 and, according to its website, crews are widening the road from two lanes to four while adding new sidewalks and lighting. Scott Samples, with the City of Port St. Lucie, said the finished project will improve both safety and traffic flow along the corridor. "We'll see a significant improvement in the safety as well as the traffic flow for this roadway," Samples said.

When asked whether city staff could put in place any temporary safety measures to address residents' concerns while construction continues, Samples said the work falls under FDOT's responsibility, not the city's. "It's tough when there is active, ongoing construction, because people still need to utilize it," Samples said. "That's why we encourage everyone to do it as safely as they possibly can." FDOT has not said whether it will add any safety measures to the corridor following last week's fatal crash.

cards.headline: Martin County Moves to Restore MARTY Bus Service With MTM Transit Deal
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners voted unanimously to negotiate a roughly $3 million, one-year contract with MTM Transit to restore MARTY bus service after last week's abrupt shutdown. County officials hope to finalize the deal by the end of the week and resume routes next week.
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator negotiate a new contract with MTM Transit to restore MARTY public bus service, days after the system abruptly shut down. The proposed deal, allowed under the county's emergency procurement rules, would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million.

MARTY service stopped last Thursday when Martin County Transit LLC, the company that had been running the system, suddenly discontinued operations. The company cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance expenses, as the reason for the shutdown. The move left several drivers, including Bill Lawrence, without jobs with no warning.

"I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners during Tuesday's meeting that county staff spent the past several days searching for a way to restore service. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county reviewed multiple proposals before settling on MTM Transit, a company that had previously operated the county's bus system, as its preferred choice. Gorton said bringing back drivers who lost their jobs in last week's shutdown is a top priority for county officials. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to begin terminating the county's contract with Martin County Transit LLC. During the one-year contract period, county officials plan to work toward a standard multi-year agreement through the county's normal competitive bidding process. County officials said they hope to finalize negotiations with MTM Transit by the end of this week, which could allow bus service to resume as soon as next week.

hero.headline: AG Vows Broader Corruption Crackdown After Fort Pierce Mimms Conviction
hero.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is promising a broader crackdown on public corruption following the conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms. A jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct but acquitted him of bid tampering in a case centered on two vacant, city-owned parcels in Fort Pierce and a nonprofit connected to Mimms' niece, who served on the organization's board.

Prosecutors said Mimms used his position to benefit the nonprofit, which received a $500,000 grant from a Catholic charitable organization for a community center that was never built. Prosecutors said Mimms later concealed his involvement in steering the award. Uthmeier said the evidence showed that "shenanigans took place" to ensure the nonprofit received the grant and that Mimms ultimately covered up his role. "He will be punished for abusing his office," Uthmeier said.

Uthmeier pointed to the conviction as an example of the state's broader effort to hold public officials accountable and said his office's Public Corruption Unit has more than 25 active investigations or cases underway. He described the Mimms case as the first of many public corruption cases the state expects to announce. "We want to ensure the public that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take," Uthmeier said.

Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Larry Keefe said his agency is making public corruption investigations a priority. "No one is too big, no one is too powerful to be held accountable," Keefe said. Official misconduct is a third-degree felony punishable by up to five years in prison. Mimms is scheduled to be sentenced in December.

cards.headline: Otto Lenke Sentenced to Death for Fort Pierce Murder of Richard Benson
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce judge formally sentenced Otto Lenke to death for the 2021 murder of motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson. Lenke's sentence will now undergo an automatic review by the Florida Supreme Court.
cards.body:
Otto Lenke was formally sentenced to death Wednesday for the 2021 murder of Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, a killing that drew out through years of court proceedings before reaching this conclusion. Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn handed down the sentence, telling Lenke directly that the court's independent evaluation of the case led to the conclusion that death was the appropriate and just sentence for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson. Lenke sat motionless in the courtroom as the judge read the ruling.

Lenke, 67, was convicted in May 2026 of first-degree murder and arson in Benson's death. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank's Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators said the motive stemmed from a personal relationship: Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke, and prosecutors argued at trial that jealousy drove Lenke to kill him because he could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past.

Prosecutors said Lenke carefully planned the murder, using a car that day that belonged to his daughter so it would not be associated with him, and later cut up the gun used in the shooting and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, did not testify in his own defense during the trial.

Assistant prosecutors Brandon White and Justin Cormier said they were relieved by the judge's decision. White said Lenke would spend the rest of his life in solitary confinement until his death and that Benson's family had finally gotten justice after years of waiting. Cormier said prosecutors respected the judge's ruling and were glad justice could be served. Skip Thompson, a friend who worked with Benson at his motorcycle shop and attended every day of the trial, said he was glad Lenke received the death penalty but was concerned the case could return to court multiple times through the appeals process. Florida law requires the state Supreme Court to automatically review every death sentence, meaning Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That review process could take years.

cards.headline: After Fatal Crash, Port St. Lucie Neighbors Push for Lighting on Port St. Lucie Boulevard
cards.teaser: Following a deadly crash, residents along Port St. Lucie Boulevard say the road still needs street lights, even as a state widening project adds sidewalks and lanes.
cards.body:
Residents along Port St. Lucie Boulevard are calling for street lighting after a fatal crash on the roadway last week. Neighbors say the stretch lacks adequate lighting at night and in the early morning hours, creating a hazard for pedestrians, drivers and schoolchildren who walk the area.

Howard Shapiro, who lives nearby, said he avoids walking in the area after dark because there are no lights. "I don't walk around here... no lighting outside at nighttime. Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there," Shapiro said. He said a new sidewalk under construction will help, but lighting needs to follow. "They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's gonna be helpful. But street lights need to follow," he said.

The Florida Department of Transportation is overseeing a project on a segment of Port St. Lucie Boulevard between Alcantara Boulevard and Parr Drive. Construction began in 2025, and according to FDOT, crews are widening the road from two lanes to four while adding new sidewalks and lighting. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said the completed project will improve safety. "We'll see a significant improvement in the safety as well as the traffic flow for this roadway," Samples said.

When asked whether the city could provide temporary safety measures while construction continues, Samples said the work falls under FDOT's responsibility. "It's tough when there is active, ongoing construction, because people still need to utilize it," Samples said. "That's why we encourage everyone to do it as safely as they possibly can."

cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a site plan application Monday for a new Costco store in the Southern Grove district, advancing a project tied to a $6 million land sale agreed to earlier this year. The approval brings the long-planned store closer to completion.

The new Costco will sit east of Southwest Village Parkway and south of the newly constructed Marshall Parkway. City leaders agreed earlier this year to sell the land to Costco for $6 million.

The store will be built next to a Costco distribution center that is currently under construction in the same area. The two projects together mark a significant expansion of Costco's presence in Southern Grove, a growing commercial corridor in Port St. Lucie.

With the site plan now approved, the project moves into its next phase of development. No opening date has been announced for the new store.

hero.headline: AG Vows Wider Corruption Crackdown After Fort Pierce City Manager's Conviction
hero.teaser: Former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms was convicted of official misconduct in a case tied to a nonprofit linked to his niece and a $500,000 grant. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier says it is the first of many public corruption cases the state expects to bring.
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms of official misconduct while acquitting him of bid tampering, in a case centered on two vacant, city-owned parcels and a nonprofit connected to his niece. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position to benefit the nonprofit and later concealed his involvement. His niece served on the nonprofit's board, and the organization received a $500,000 grant from a Catholic charitable organization for a community center that was never built.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is pointing to the conviction as he pledges a broader crackdown on public corruption across the state. "We want to ensure the public that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take," Uthmeier said. He said the evidence showed that "shenanigans took place" to ensure the nonprofit received the award and that Mimms ultimately covered up his involvement.

"He will be punished for abusing his office," Uthmeier said. The attorney general said his office's Public Corruption Unit has more than 25 active investigations or cases underway and described the Mimms case as the first of many public corruption cases the state expects to announce. Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Larry Keefe said his agency is making public corruption investigations a priority. "No one is too big, no one is too powerful to be held accountable," Keefe said.

Official misconduct is a third-degree felony punishable by up to five years in prison. Mimms is scheduled to be sentenced in December.

cards.headline: Otto Lenke Formally Sentenced to Death for Fort Pierce Murder of Richard Benson
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County circuit judge formally sentenced Otto Lenke to death Wednesday for the 2021 killing of Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, a case that began when Lenke shot Benson and then set him on fire while he was still alive. Lenke, 67, was convicted of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026. Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn imposed the sentence at a hearing, telling Lenke directly that the court's independent evaluation led to the conclusion that death was the appropriate and just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson.

"The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," Judge Linn said. Lenke sat motionless in the courtroom as he learned his fate. He did not testify in his own defense during the trial.

Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank's Custom Cycle Components, just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. Investigators said the motive stemmed from a personal relationship: Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke, and prosecutors argued at trial that jealousy over that relationship fueled the killing. Prosecutors said Lenke carefully planned the murder, using a car that day belonging to his daughter so people would not associate him with it, and later cut up the gun used in the shooting and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter.

Assistant State Attorneys Brandon White and Justin Cormier both said they were relieved by the outcome. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," White said. Cormier added, "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served." Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop and attended every day of the trial, said he supported the sentence but was wary of the appeals ahead. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," Thompson said. Florida law requires the state Supreme Court to review every death sentence, giving Lenke an automatic legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence, a process that could take years.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Woman Pleads Guilty to Exploiting Elderly Boca Raton Client
cards.teaser: Rachel Albert diverted nearly $20,000 from an elderly client through fraudulent checks and unauthorized credit card purchases. She was sentenced to jail time, probation and ordered to pay restitution.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie woman pleaded guilty Wednesday to exploiting an elderly client in Boca Raton, after prosecutors said she diverted nearly $20,000 from the victim through fraudulent checks and unauthorized credit card purchases. Rachel R. Albert, 57, entered the plea in a Palm Beach County courtroom to a charge of exploitation of an elderly person or disabled adult, according to court documents.

Albert was sentenced to 364 days in the Palm Beach County jail and credited with 33 days already served. She will also serve three years of probation. The court ordered her to pay restitution to the victim and cover court costs.

According to a Boca Raton Police Department arrest report, Albert had access between November 2023 and October 2024 to the checkbook belonging to the victim and the victim's daughter. She wrote fraudulent checks totaling $15,330 and deposited them into her own bank account. Albert also had access to the victim's credit card for necessary purchases, but made unauthorized personal purchases totaling $2,711.35 on the card.

As part of her sentence, Albert is barred from contacting the victim, the victim's family or their property. She is also prohibited from working as a home health aide or in any capacity caring for a disabled adult or elderly person as defined under state law, including through a third party. The state attorney's office declined to pursue two additional counts of fraudulent use of personal identification information against Albert.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police Investigate Death of Man Found in Lincoln Park Lake
cards.teaser: A man in his 30s was pulled dead from a lake at Lincoln Park in Fort Pierce Wednesday morning, and police are still working to notify his next of kin while they investigate how he ended up in the water.
cards.body:
A man in his 30s was found dead in a lake at Lincoln Park in Fort Pierce Wednesday morning, and police are investigating how he ended up in the water. A citizen flagged down an officer just after 9 a.m. after spotting a body floating in the lake near the 400 block of North 13th Street, according to Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago. Officers arrived and found the man face down in the water. Rescue crews pulled him from the lake, but he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Police have identified the man but are waiting to notify his next of kin before releasing his name. Santiago described him as a Black man believed to be between 30 and 32 years old. Investigators are trying to determine how he entered the water and what he was doing beforehand.

Santiago said there were no apparent signs of trauma on the man's body, though it appeared to have been in the water for some time. Police are canvassing the Lincoln Park area, speaking with potential witnesses and searching for surveillance footage that could help explain how the man ended up in the lake. Investigators are also looking into whether currents in the waterway could have carried the body to where it was found.

It is too early to determine whether foul play or drugs played a role in the man's death, Santiago said. Police are waiting on the medical examiner's findings, including autopsy and toxicology results, to help determine the cause of death.
